The entire process eliminates the need for graph pooling layers, thus preserving more structural information and reducing model complexity.
ad720ec891fd143090de390a2e800eb8e9e6eb4d.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on 14 diverse datasets spanning domains such as social networks, biology, co-authorship, transportation, and power networks. Both plain and attributed graphs will be considered. The proposed method will be compared against several baselines, including high-order heuristic methods (Katz, PageRank, SimRank), node embedding methods (node2vec), and the state-of-the-art deep learning model SEAL. Evaluation metrics will include Area Under the Curve (AUC) and Average Precision (AP). The experimental setup involves randomly splitting each dataset into training and testing sets with varying proportions (e.g., 50% and 80% training links), and negative samples are generated by randomly selecting non-existent links. Hyperparameters for all methods will be tuned for optimal performance, and the number of epochs, architecture details, and parameter counts will be controlled for fair comparison. Convergence speed and parameter efficiency will also be analyzed.
ad720ec891fd143090de390a2e800eb8e9e6eb4d.novelty_claims: The proposed method is the first to systematically convert the link prediction problem into a node classification task in the line graph, enabling direct feature learning for candidate links without the need for graph pooling layers. This approach preserves more information from the original graph structure, reduces the number of model parameters, and significantly accelerates training convergence. Experimental results are expected to demonstrate consistent outperformance over all baselines, including the current state-of-the-art, across a wide range of datasets and settings.

ad77501bd6d6359a3d18a8d2af80651d5046d12e.title: Homomorphism-Distinguishing Closedness for Graphs of Bounded Tree-Width
ad77501bd6d6359a3d18a8d2af80651d5046d12e.research_question: Which graph classes closed under minors and disjoint unions are homomorphism-distinguishing closed, and how does this property relate to the ability of the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm to detect subgraph counts for graphs of bounded tree-width?
ad77501bd6d6359a3d18a8d2af80651d5046d12e.hypothesis: Every class of graphs closed under taking minors and disjoint unions is homomorphism-distinguishing closed, and for all k ≥ 1, the class of graphs of tree-width at most k is homomorphism-distinguishing closed. Furthermore, the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm detects exactly those subgraph counts whose hereditary tree-width is at most k.
ad77501bd6d6359a3d18a8d2af80651d5046d12e.proposed_method: The proposed research will establish homomorphism-distinguishing closedness for all classes of graphs of bounded tree-width by leveraging game-theoretic characterizations (such as the cops-and-robber game and the bijective pebble game) and algebraic tools involving homomorphism counts and oddomorphisms. The approach will utilize the CFI (Cai-Fürer-Immerman) construction to generate pairs of graphs that are indistinguishable by homomorphism counts from bounded tree-width graphs but can be separated by specific homomorphism counts. The proof will be structured by verifying the necessary closure properties and employing lemmas that connect weak oddomorphisms, minors, and the existence of distinguishing homomorphism counts. Additionally, the research will characterize the subgraph counts detectable by the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm by expressing subgraph counts as linear combinations of homomorphism counts and relating them to hereditary tree-width.
ad77501bd6d6359a3d18a8d2af80651d5046d12e.experiment_details: Theoretical validation will be conducted by constructing explicit pairs of non-isomorphic graphs using the CFI construction and analyzing their homomorphism counts with respect to classes of bounded tree-width. The research will employ combinatorial games (cops-and-robber and bijective pebble games) to establish indistinguishability and use algebraic arguments to demonstrate the existence of distinguishing subgraph counts. The evaluation will include a complete classification of subgraph patterns detected by the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm, with hereditary tree-width as the key parameter. No empirical datasets are used, as the results are proven in a purely mathematical and combinatorial framework. Baselines for comparison include previously known results for k = 1, 2 and for specific subgraph patterns.
ad77501bd6d6359a3d18a8d2af80651d5046d12e.novelty_claims: This research confirms a conjecture that all graph classes closed under minors and disjoint unions are homomorphism-distinguishing closed for the case of bounded tree-width, generalizing prior results limited to small k. It provides a complete and tight classification of which subgraph counts are detected by the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm for all k, resolving an open question in the literature. The approach unifies algebraic, combinatorial, and game-theoretic techniques to establish new connections between graph homomorphism counts, tree-width, and algorithmic graph isomorphism heuristics.

ad91394aaa1dad451e1ea52acb73b525c9574642.title: Depthwise Hyperparameter Transfer in Residual Networks: Dynamics and Scaling Limit
ad91394aaa1dad451e1ea52acb73b525c9574642.research_question: Can hyperparameters, such as learning rate, momentum, and regularization strength, be transferred simultaneously across both width and depth in deep residual neural networks, including convolutional ResNets and Vision Transformers, and what are the theoretical and empirical conditions that enable such transfer?
ad91394aaa1dad451e1ea52acb73b525c9574642.hypothesis: A specific parameterization of residual networks, combining μP scaling with a residual branch scaling factor of 1/sqrt(depth), enables consistent transfer of optimal hyperparameters across both width and depth, supported by a well-defined joint infinite-width and infinite-depth limit in learning dynamics.
ad91394aaa1dad451e1ea52acb73b525c9574642.proposed_method: A novel parameterization for residual networks is developed, where the residual branch is scaled by 1/sqrt(L) (with L being the network depth), and μP scaling is applied to the weights and learning rates. The architecture is defined as a sequence of residual blocks, each with the scaling factor applied to the residual connection, and the weights are initialized according to μP principles. The learning rate and output scaling are chosen to ensure that feature and prediction updates are invariant to both width and depth. Theoretical analysis is conducted using dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) to characterize the joint infinite-width and infinite-depth limit, ensuring that the dynamics and feature learning remain consistent as the network scales. Both convolutional and transformer-based residual architectures are considered, with and without normalization layers, and the method is compatible with various optimizers such as SGD and Adam.
ad91394aaa1dad451e1ea52acb73b525c9574642.experiment_details: Experiments are performed on CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet datasets using both convolutional ResNets and Vision Transformers. Networks of varying widths and depths are trained, and hyperparameter transfer is assessed by measuring the consistency of optimal learning rates, momentum, and regularization strengths across different model sizes. Baselines include standard parameterization (PyTorch default), μP parameterization, and versions with normalization layers (BatchNorm, LayerNorm). Evaluation metrics include training and test loss, accuracy, and the convergence of learning dynamics across architectures. Learning rate schedules such as linear warm-up and cosine annealing are also tested for transferability. Theoretical predictions are validated by comparing finite-size network dynamics to the DMFT-derived infinite-width/depth limit, and convergence rates are empirically measured.
ad91394aaa1dad451e1ea52acb73b525c9574642.novelty_claims: The proposed approach is the first to demonstrate consistent transfer of optimal hyperparameters across both width and depth in residual networks by combining μP parameterization with a 1/sqrt(depth) residual branch scaling. The method is empirically validated across multiple architectures and datasets, and is supported by a new theoretical analysis using DMFT that establishes the existence of a well-defined joint infinite-width and infinite-depth feature learning limit. The approach enables significant reductions in computational cost for hyperparameter tuning in large-scale deep learning models, and provides a principled framework for scaling neural networks while maintaining consistent training dynamics.

ad934a9344f68fcc0b9aa704102aa48c39c5b591.title: Generating with Confidence: Uncertainty Quantification for Black-box Large Language Models
ad934a9344f68fcc0b9aa704102aa48c39c5b591.research_question: How can uncertainty and confidence in responses generated by black-box large language models (LLMs) be effectively quantified and used to improve the reliability of natural language generation, particularly in scenarios where only the generated text is accessible and not the internal model outputs?
ad934a9344f68fcc0b9aa704102aa48c39c5b591.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that uncertainty and confidence in black-box LLM outputs can be reliably estimated using measures derived from the semantic dispersion of multiple generated responses, and that these measures can outperform existing baselines, including some white-box approaches, in identifying unreliable generations.
ad934a9344f68fcc0b9aa704102aa48c39c5b591.proposed_method: The proposed methodology involves generating multiple responses from a black-box LLM for each input prompt and computing pairwise semantic similarities between these responses using both rule-based (Jaccard similarity) and model-based (Natural Language Inference, NLI) approaches. Several uncertainty and confidence measures are then constructed: (1) the number of semantic equivalence sets among responses (NumSet), (2) spectral clustering-based metrics such as the sum of eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian (EigV), (3) node degree-based metrics (Deg), and (4) eccentricity in the spectral embedding space (Ecc). These measures are designed to capture both input-level uncertainty and response-specific confidence without requiring access to token-level logits or internal model states. The NLI model used for semantic similarity is a smaller, off-the-shelf classifier, ensuring practicality for black-box settings.
ad934a9344f68fcc0b9aa704102aa48c39c5b591.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on several question-answering datasets, including CoQA, TriviaQA, and Natural Questions, using a range of LLMs such as OPT-13B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA2-13B, and GPT-3.5-turbo (API access only). For each question, multiple responses (e.g., 20) will be generated, and the proposed uncertainty/confidence measures will be computed. Baselines will include existing black-box and white-box uncertainty quantification methods, such as semantic entropy and model self-reported confidence. Evaluation will focus on the ability of each measure to predict response correctness, using metrics like AUROC and AUARC (Area Under Accuracy-Rejection Curve), with correctness judged via automated scoring (using GPT-3.5-turbo) and validated by human annotation. The impact of varying the number of generated samples will also be assessed.
ad934a9344f68fcc0b9aa704102aa48c39c5b591.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces a suite of simple, practical uncertainty and confidence measures for black-box LLMs that do not require access to internal model outputs. It leverages semantic similarity via NLI models to quantify dispersion among generated responses, enabling both input-level and response-level uncertainty estimation. The approach is designed for realistic deployment scenarios where only generated text is available, and demonstrates that these black-box measures can match or exceed the performance of white-box baselines in selective natural language generation tasks.

ad9bac9b786f65f0a832b11ba7e83639c90da415.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
ad9bac9b786f65f0a832b11ba7e83639c90da415.research_question: What are the underlying dynamical mechanisms that give rise to neural scaling laws in deep learning, and how do training time, model size, and dataset size interact to determine the optimal allocation of computational resources for model performance?
ad9bac9b786f65f0a832b11ba7e83639c90da415.hypothesis: Neural scaling laws can be explained by the learning dynamics of random feature models, and the exponents governing scaling with training time, model size, and dataset size are generally distinct and determined by the spectral properties of the data and model architecture. As a result, the compute-optimal strategy involves an asymmetric scaling of model size and training time, and feature learning can further accelerate scaling beyond what is predicted by linearized models.
ad9bac9b786f65f0a832b11ba7e83639c90da415.proposed_method: A mathematically tractable dynamical model will be developed based on a random feature (linearized) neural network trained with gradient descent. The model will be analyzed in both continuous-time (gradient flow) and discrete-time (SGD) regimes, allowing for explicit variation of training time, model size (width), and dataset size. Dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) will be employed to derive closed-form equations for the evolution of train and test loss, as well as response and correlation functions that characterize the learning dynamics. The model will incorporate power-law structured features in the data, enabling analytical derivation of scaling exponents for loss as a function of time, model size, and dataset size. Extensions will include the effects of ensembling, finite batch size, and the transition from kernel (lazy) to feature-learning regimes.
ad9bac9b786f65f0a832b11ba7e83639c90da415.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on both synthetic datasets with controlled power-law spectral properties and on realistic datasets such as CIFAR-5M and Wikitext-100M. Neural network architectures including residual CNNs and transformers will be evaluated in both the linearized (kernel) and feature-learning regimes. Baselines will include varying model width, training time, and dataset size, as well as ensembling and bagging strategies. Evaluation metrics will focus on test and train loss, scaling exponents, and the compute-optimal Pareto frontier. Empirical results will be compared to theoretical predictions from the DMFT analysis, and the impact of feature learning on scaling laws will be investigated by comparing kernel and feature-learning models.
ad9bac9b786f65f0a832b11ba7e83639c90da415.novelty_claims: The proposed model provides a unified dynamical framework that explains the emergence of neural scaling laws and their exponents in terms of training dynamics, model size, and data structure. It predicts and analytically derives the asymmetry between model size and training time exponents in compute-optimal scaling, a phenomenon observed empirically but not previously explained theoretically. The approach also elucidates why ensembling is suboptimal compared to increasing model size, and quantifies the gradual buildup of overfitting due to data reuse. Furthermore, the model offers a theoretical interpretation of how feature learning can accelerate scaling beyond the predictions of linearized models, and provides practical guidance for allocating computational resources in large-scale deep learning.

ad9effaa6c12330f24e34bd3fa5d1496acc113af.title: More Than a Toy: Random Matrix Models Predict How Real-World Neural Representations Generalize
ad9effaa6c12330f24e34bd3fa5d1496acc113af.research_question: What theoretical assumptions are necessary or sufficient to capture the qualitative phenomena of generalization in large-scale, overparameterized machine learning models, particularly in the context of neural representations derived from real-world data? How can the generalization behavior of kernel regression on neural representations be accurately predicted and explained, and what factors govern scaling laws and the effectiveness of pretraining?
ad9effaa6c12330f24e34bd3fa5d1496acc113af.hypothesis: Random matrix theory, specifically the validity of a local Marchenko-Pastur law, provides a sufficient framework to accurately predict the generalization risk of high-dimensional ridge regression on neural representations, even in overparameterized and realistic data settings. Alignment between the ground truth function and the population covariance eigenbasis, rather than just eigenvalue decay or norm-based measures, is necessary to explain the generalization and scaling behavior observed in practice.
ad9effaa6c12330f24e34bd3fa5d1496acc113af.proposed_method: A novel framework will be developed to analyze generalization in high-dimensional linear models derived from neural network representations, focusing on empirical neural tangent kernels (eNTKs) extracted from large-scale, possibly pretrained, neural networks. The methodology will involve benchmarking the predictive accuracy of the Generalized Cross-Validation (GCV) estimator for generalization risk across a wide range of datasets, model architectures, and regularization strengths. Theoretical analysis will be conducted to prove non-asymptotic bounds on the error of the GCV estimator under a local random matrix law, extending previous random matrix results to settings with highly anisotropic covariates and large-norm ground truth functions. Additionally, principled, sample-efficient estimators for alignment and eigenvalue decay will be developed, enabling accurate prediction of scaling law exponents from empirical data.
ad9effaa6c12330f24e34bd3fa5d1496acc113af.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using eNTK representations from various ResNet architectures (e.g., ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ResNet-101) on multiple vision datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, Flowers-102, and Food-101. Both randomly initialized and ImageNet-pretrained networks will be evaluated. Kernel regression on eNTKs will be compared to regression on last-layer activations and full-network finetuning using SGD. The GCV estimator's predictions will be quantitatively compared to actual generalization risk, as well as to norm-based and spectrum-based baselines, using correlation and scaling law exponent estimation as evaluation metrics. Experiments will systematically vary dataset size (N) and ridge regularization (λ), and will include analysis of the convergence properties of the empirical covariance and the impact of pretraining on alignment and eigenvalue decay.
ad9effaa6c12330f24e34bd3fa5d1496acc113af.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces the first non-asymptotic theoretical analysis of the GCV estimator for generalization risk in high-dimensional, realistic neural representations, applicable beyond the classical regime and without restrictive assumptions on the ground truth norm or data distribution. It demonstrates that random matrix theory, rather than traditional norm- or spectrum-based approaches, is central to understanding generalization in neural representations. The approach provides new, sample-efficient estimators for alignment and eigenvalue decay, and shows empirically and theoretically that these quantities are sufficient to predict scaling law exponents for kernel regression. The findings challenge the prevailing intuition that pretraining improves generalization by reducing effective dimension, instead highlighting the critical role of alignment. A scalable software library for large-scale empirical NTK computation is also developed.

adb272fbdea3631059cf88ab764bb6c2ce29f965.title: Visual Prompt Tuning
adb272fbdea3631059cf88ab764bb6c2ce29f965.research_question: How can large pre-trained vision Transformer models be efficiently and effectively adapted to a wide variety of downstream visual recognition tasks without full fine-tuning of all backbone parameters?
adb272fbdea3631059cf88ab764bb6c2ce29f965.hypothesis: Introducing a small set of learnable prompt parameters into the input space of a frozen pre-trained vision Transformer enables parameter-efficient adaptation to downstream tasks, achieving competitive or superior performance compared to full fine-tuning and other parameter-efficient methods.
adb272fbdea3631059cf88ab764bb6c2ce29f965.proposed_method: A new adaptation technique, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT), is proposed for large-scale vision Transformers. VPT introduces a small number of learnable prompt embeddings into the input sequence of the Transformer, while keeping the backbone weights frozen during downstream training. Two variants are explored: VPT-shallow, where prompts are prepended only to the first layer's input, and VPT-deep, where prompts are inserted at the input of every Transformer layer. Only the prompt parameters and the classification head are updated per task, minimizing per-task storage requirements. The prompts are optimized jointly with the head using standard supervised objectives, and the approach is compatible with different Transformer architectures (e.g., ViT, Swin) and scales.
adb272fbdea3631059cf88ab764bb6c2ce29f965.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) and Swin Transformer backbones, both trained on ImageNet-21k. The method will be evaluated on 24 downstream recognition tasks, including five fine-grained visual classification (FGVC) datasets (CUB-200-2011, NABirds, Oxford Flowers, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars) and the VTAB-1k benchmark, which comprises 19 diverse visual classification tasks grouped into Natural, Specialized, and Structured categories. Baselines for comparison include full fine-tuning, linear head tuning, partial and MLP head tuning, Sidetune, Bias tuning, and Adapter methods. Evaluation metrics will be average test accuracy across tasks, and experiments will systematically vary training data size, backbone scale (ViT-Base/Large/Huge), and prompt design choices. Ablation studies will examine prompt location, prompt length, and insertion strategies.
adb272fbdea3631059cf88ab764bb6c2ce29f965.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces the first systematic framework for prompt tuning in vision Transformers, enabling adaptation by learning a small set of input-space prompts while keeping the backbone frozen. This approach achieves significant parameter efficiency, requiring less than 1% of model parameters per task, and often outperforms full fine-tuning and other parameter-efficient baselines across a wide range of tasks, data regimes, and model scales. VPT demonstrates that prompt-based adaptation is not only feasible but can surpass traditional fine-tuning strategies in vision, especially in low-data scenarios and with large-scale models.

adbe11bac1db1505d0e085c232f9aaaeb70470ac.title: UNION: Unsupervised 3D Object Detection using Object Appearance-based Pseudo-Classes
adbe11bac1db1505d0e085c232f9aaaeb70470ac.research_question: How can unsupervised 3D object detection be achieved using multi-modal sensor data, without relying on manual labels, and in a way that enables both class-agnostic and multi-class detection of static and dynamic mobile objects?
adbe11bac1db1505d0e085c232f9aaaeb70470ac.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that combining spatial clustering of LiDAR point clouds, self-supervised scene flow for motion estimation, and visual appearance embeddings from camera images can enable the discovery and classification of both static and dynamic mobile objects in an unsupervised manner, thereby eliminating the need for iterative self-training and improving detection performance.
adbe11bac1db1505d0e085c232f9aaaeb70470ac.proposed_method: The proposed method introduces a multi-stage framework that jointly leverages LiDAR, camera, and temporal information for unsupervised 3D object detection. First, non-ground points are extracted from LiDAR point clouds using RANSAC-based ground plane fitting. These points are aggregated across multiple time steps and spatially clustered using HDBSCAN to generate object proposals. Motion estimation is performed on each proposal using a modified self-supervised scene flow algorithm (ICP-Flow), classifying proposals as static or dynamic based on velocity thresholds. Visual appearance embeddings for each proposal are computed by projecting LiDAR points onto camera images and extracting features using a self-supervised vision transformer (DINOv2). These embeddings are clustered with K-Means to group visually similar objects, and clusters with a sufficient fraction of dynamic instances are labeled as mobile object clusters. Pseudo-bounding boxes and pseudo-class labels are generated for these mobile objects, enabling the training of existing 3D object detectors in a fully unsupervised manner.
adbe11bac1db1505d0e085c232f9aaaeb70470ac.experiment_details: Experiments are conducted on the nuScenes dataset, a large-scale autonomous driving benchmark with multi-modal sensor data (LiDAR and six camera views per frame). The proposed method is evaluated for both class-agnostic and multi-class 3D object detection. CenterPoint, a state-of-the-art LiDAR-based 3D object detector, is trained using the generated pseudo-labels. Baselines include unsupervised methods such as HDBSCAN, OYSTER, and LISO, as well as supervised CenterPoint models trained with 1%, 10%, and 100% of manual labels. Evaluation metrics include Average Precision (AP), nuScenes Detection Score (NDS), and true positive errors for translation, scale, orientation, and velocity. Ablation studies are performed to assess the contributions of each pipeline component and the impact of different image encoders. Multi-class detection experiments use appearance-based clustering to generate pseudo-classes, with minimal supervision for class association during inference.
adbe11bac1db1505d0e085c232f9aaaeb70470ac.novelty_claims: The proposed framework is the first to jointly exploit LiDAR, camera, and temporal information for unsupervised 3D object detection, enabling both class-agnostic and multi-class detection without iterative self-training. The method introduces an appearance-based pseudo-class labeling scheme that extends 3D object discovery to multi-class detection, leveraging visual similarity between static and dynamic mobile objects to distinguish them from background. This approach significantly reduces computational cost and training complexity, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on unsupervised 3D object discovery benchmarks, more than doubling the average precision compared to previous methods.

adc8c71591ee5b043447a7d7db8ae09a8a9f1251.title: Interpretable Preferences via Multi-Objective Reward Modeling and Mixture-of-Experts
adc8c71591ee5b043447a7d7db8ae09a8a9f1251.research_question: How can reward models for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) be made more interpretable and steerable, while maintaining or improving alignment performance for large language models (LLMs)?
adc8c71591ee5b043447a7d7db8ae09a8a9f1251.hypothesis: A multi-objective reward modeling approach, combined with a context-dependent mixture-of-experts (MoE) scalarization mechanism, will yield reward models that are both interpretable and capable of state-of-the-art alignment performance, mitigating issues such as verbosity bias and reward hacking.
adc8c71591ee5b043447a7d7db8ae09a8a9f1251.proposed_method: A two-stage methodology is proposed. First, an Absolute-Rating Multi-Objective Reward Model (ArmoRM) is trained using multi-dimensional absolute-rating data, where each dimension corresponds to a human-interpretable objective (e.g., helpfulness, honesty, safety, verbosity). The model uses a pre-trained LLM backbone (e.g., Llama-3 8B) as a feature extractor, with a linear regression layer trained to predict the k-dimensional objective ratings from the final hidden state. Second, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) gating network is introduced, which takes prompt features and outputs non-negative coefficients (via a shallow MLP and softmax) to scalarize the multi-objective outputs into a single reward score. The gating network is trained with the backbone and regression layer frozen, using the Bradley-Terry loss on pairwise preference data. Additionally, a verbosity bias correction is applied to each objective using a penalty term based on correlation metrics, ensuring that the scalarized reward is less susceptible to verbosity bias.
adc8c71591ee5b043447a7d7db8ae09a8a9f1251.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using the Llama-3 8B architecture, initializing the backbone from a pre-trained Bradley-Terry reward model. The ArmoRM is trained with regression loss on 19 objectives from 8 datasets, while the MoE gating layer is trained on 10 pairwise preference datasets using the AdamW optimizer and a batch size of 1024. Evaluation will be performed on RewardBench, a benchmark designed to assess reward models for LLM alignment across categories such as Chat, Chat Hard, Safety, Reasoning, and Prior Sets, with weighted average accuracy as the primary metric. Baselines for comparison include Bradley-Terry models, LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4), and other multi-objective reward models. Hardware includes CPUs for linear probing and a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU for gating layer training.
adc8c71591ee5b043447a7d7db8ae09a8a9f1251.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces a multi-objective reward modeling framework that leverages fine-grained, interpretable absolute ratings rather than coarse pairwise preferences, preserving more information about human judgment. The use of a context-dependent MoE gating network for scalarization allows dynamic adjustment of reward objective weights based on prompt features, improving steerability and robustness. The method incorporates a principled correction for verbosity bias, addressing a common failure mode in reward models. The approach is claimed to achieve state-of-the-art performance on RewardBench, outperforming both similarly sized and much larger existing reward models, as well as LLM-as-a-judge methods.

add7c86e21051a5d9f8509876a0b26b9905af765.title: Group DETR: Fast DETR Training with Group-Wise One-to-Many Assignment
add7c86e21051a5d9f8509876a0b26b9905af765.research_question: How can the training efficiency and convergence speed of detection transformer (DETR) models be improved without sacrificing end-to-end performance or requiring post-processing steps such as non-maximum suppression (NMS)?
add7c86e21051a5d9f8509876a0b26b9905af765.hypothesis: Introducing a group-wise one-to-many assignment mechanism, where multiple groups of object queries are used during training with one-to-one assignment within each group and separate self-attention, will provide more supervision, stabilize training, and accelerate convergence of DETR-based models, while maintaining or improving detection accuracy.
add7c86e21051a5d9f8509876a0b26b9905af765.proposed_method: A novel training framework is proposed for DETR-based object detectors that employs K groups of object queries, where each group contains N queries. During training, one-to-one assignment is performed within each group, so each ground-truth object is assigned to one prediction per group, resulting in one-to-many assignment overall. Decoder self-attention is performed separately within each group, eliminating interference between groups and ensuring that competition for ground-truth assignment occurs only within a group. The decoder and predictor parameters are shared across groups, and the loss is aggregated over all groups. During inference, only a single group of queries is used, and no architectural changes or post-processing (such as NMS) are required. This approach is compatible with various DETR variants and can be implemented efficiently using parallel self-attention and memory-efficient attention mechanisms.
add7c86e21051a5d9f8509876a0b26b9905af765.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on the COCO 2017 dataset for object detection and instance segmentation, using standard backbones such as ResNet-50 and large-scale backbones like Swin-Large and ViT-Huge. Baseline models will include Conditional DETR, DAB-DETR, DN-DETR, DAB-Deformable-DETR, and DINO, as well as Mask2Former for segmentation and PETR/PETRv2 for 3D detection on nuScenes. Evaluation metrics will include mean average precision (mAP) for detection and segmentation, and nuScenes Detection Score (NDS) for 3D detection. Training schedules will range from 12 to 50 epochs, and comparisons will be made with and without the proposed group-wise assignment. Additional ablation studies will analyze the effects of group number, separate self-attention, and assignment strategies. Training time, GPU memory usage, and convergence speed will also be measured.
add7c86e21051a5d9f8509876a0b26b9905af765.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces a group-wise one-to-many assignment scheme for DETR training, enabling more supervision and faster convergence without requiring architectural changes or NMS at inference. The approach is simple, general, and applicable to a wide range of DETR variants, including strong baselines and related tasks such as 3D detection and instance segmentation. It is the first to demonstrate that group-wise assignment with separate self-attention can stabilize DETR training and improve both encoder and decoder learning. The method achieves significant improvements in training speed and accuracy, and is compatible with memory-efficient implementations for practical scalability.

adf27e97f219b8bf4a81644f016a86d5a1034b47.title: Fast, Differentiable and Sparse Top-k: a Convex Analysis Perspective
adf27e97f219b8bf4a81644f016a86d5a1034b47.research_question: How can a top-k operator be designed to be both differentiable and sparse, enabling its effective integration into neural networks for tasks such as weight pruning, top-k loss optimization, and routing in mixture-of-experts models?
adf27e97f219b8bf4a81644f016a86d5a1034b47.hypothesis: Introducing a convex analysis-based framework for the top-k operator, incorporating p-norm regularization and nonlinear mappings, will yield operators that are differentiable (or differentiable almost everywhere), sparse, and computationally efficient, thereby improving performance in neural network training and inference tasks compared to existing hard or non-sparse relaxations.
adf27e97f219b8bf4a81644f016a86d5a1034b47.proposed_method: A generalized framework will be developed that formulates the top-k operator as a linear program over the permutahedron, the convex hull of all permutations of a vector. The method introduces a nonlinear mapping φ(x) to allow for flexible operator definitions, including top-k in magnitude, and incorporates a p-norm regularization term (with p between 1 and 2) to achieve differentiability and sparsity. The computation of the regularized operator will be reduced to isotonic optimization, enabling efficient solutions via the Pool Adjacent Violator (PAV) algorithm or a newly proposed, GPU/TPU-friendly Dykstra projection algorithm. Closed-form expressions for the Jacobian of the operator will be derived to facilitate efficient gradient computation during backpropagation.
adf27e97f219b8bf4a81644f016a86d5a1034b47.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted in three domains: (1) weight pruning in neural networks, where a multilayer perceptron (MLP) is trained on MNIST with 90% of weights pruned using the differentiable top-k operator, and results are compared to hard top-k and entropy-regularized baselines; (2) fine-tuning vision transformers (ViT-B/16) on CIFAR100 using a smooth, sparse top-k loss instead of cross-entropy, evaluating top-k accuracy for various values of k; and (3) routing in sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, where the differentiable top-k operator is used as a router in a vision MoE (V-MoE) trained on the large-scale JFT-300M dataset, with validation precision-at-1 compared to the hard top-k baseline. Evaluation metrics include test error, top-k accuracy, and precision-at-1, and experiments are run on both CPU and TPU hardware to assess computational efficiency.
adf27e97f219b8bf4a81644f016a86d5a1034b47.novelty_claims: The proposed approach is the first to provide a top-k operator that is both differentiable everywhere (or almost everywhere) and sparse, with a principled convex analysis foundation. The framework generalizes previous methods by supporting nonlinear mappings and p-norm regularization, enabling new operators such as top-k in magnitude and establishing connections to k-support and OWL norms. The introduction of a GPU/TPU-friendly Dykstra algorithm for isotonic optimization offers significant computational advantages for large-scale neural network applications. Empirical results demonstrate improved convergence speed, accuracy, and practical applicability in pruning, loss optimization, and mixture-of-experts routing compared to existing hard and non-sparse differentiable top-k relaxations.

adfb4da6e23df01031e3cb577e5583b4c8f321cd.title: LEVIS: Large Exact Verifiable Input Spaces for Neural Networks
adfb4da6e23df01031e3cb577e5583b4c8f321cd.research_question: How can large, exact, and verifiable input regions for neural networks be identified and characterized, such that all points within these regions are guaranteed to be free from adversarial examples and satisfy specified output criteria, especially in high-dimensional, non-convex, and potentially discontinuous input spaces?
adfb4da6e23df01031e3cb577e5583b4c8f321cd.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that a combination of mixed-integer programming (MIP) and complementarity-constrained (CC) optimization can be leveraged to efficiently and accurately identify large, exact verifiable input regions for neural networks, and that these methods can scale to high-dimensional and complex input spaces while providing global optimality guarantees.
adfb4da6e23df01031e3cb577e5583b4c8f321cd.proposed_method: A novel framework, LEVIS, is proposed to identify large, exact verifiable input spaces for neural networks. The approach consists of two main algorithms: LEVIS-α, which iteratively searches for a single, large verifiable ball that touches at least two boundaries of the verifiable region, and LEVIS-β, which systematically aggregates multiple verifiable balls to cover the entire verifiable input space. The methodology formulates the search for the largest verifiable ball as a mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem, encoding ReLU activations with integer variables and leveraging global optimization. To improve scalability, a complementarity-constrained (CC) relaxation is introduced, replacing integer variables with continuous ones and reducing computational complexity while maintaining near-global optimality. Directional adversarial search is incorporated to guide the expansion of verifiable regions, and the algorithms dynamically update ball centers based on adversarial points found along specified directions. The framework is designed to be parallelizable and adaptable to different norms and search strategies.
adfb4da6e23df01031e3cb577e5583b4c8f321cd.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on both regression and classification tasks, including optimal power flow (OPF) regression using the IEEE 9-bus power grid benchmark and image classification using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Neural networks with three layers and ReLU activations will be trained for each task. The proposed methods will be compared against baselines such as Lipschitz-based lower bounds and existing MIP-based verifiers (e.g., CROWN). Evaluation metrics will include the size (radius) of the verifiable region, computational runtime, and optimality gap. The experiments will also analyze the geometric properties of the discovered verifiable regions using visualization techniques (e.g., t-SNE) and will assess the distribution and coverage of verifiable balls under different search directions, initialization shifts, and random seeds. Multiple runs and random initializations will be used to ensure robustness and generalizability of the findings.
adfb4da6e23df01031e3cb577e5583b4c8f321cd.novelty_claims: The proposed framework introduces the first scalable and exact method for identifying large, adversarial-free input regions for neural networks using a combination of MIP and CC optimization. Unlike prior work that focuses on output verification for predefined input domains or over-approximates verifiable regions, this approach directly characterizes and expands the verifiable input space itself, providing global optimality guarantees and exact coverage. The method achieves significant computational speedup (up to 6x) over traditional MIP approaches and enables visualization and analysis of the geometric structure of verifiable input regions. The framework is adaptable to high-dimensional, non-convex, and discontinuous input spaces and is demonstrated to outperform existing baselines in both efficiency and the size of verified regions.

ae16c93bf3a33c43e8f57293530069e77c89bcaa.title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers
ae16c93bf3a33c43e8f57293530069e77c89bcaa.research_question: How can the robustness and alignment of AI systems, including large language models, multimodal models, and AI agents, be improved to reliably prevent the generation of harmful outputs, even in the presence of strong and unforeseen adversarial attacks, without sacrificing model utility?
ae16c93bf3a33c43e8f57293530069e77c89bcaa.hypothesis: Directly controlling and rerouting internal model representations responsible for harmful outputs using circuit breakers will significantly reduce harmful behaviors and increase adversarial robustness, while preserving or minimally impacting the model's capabilities.
ae16c93bf3a33c43e8f57293530069e77c89bcaa.proposed_method: A novel circuit-breaking framework will be developed that operates on internal neural representations associated with harmful outputs. The approach, termed Representation Rerouting (RR), utilizes representation engineering to remap the model's internal activations—when they correspond to harmful processes—towards incoherent or refusal representations, effectively 'short-circuiting' the harmful generation process. The method will employ Low-Rank Representation Adaptation (LoRRA) to introduce trainable adapters, and optimize a loss function that enforces orthogonality between harmful and benign representations while retaining desirable behaviors. Training will use two datasets: a Circuit Breaker Set (examples eliciting harmful representations) and a Retain Set (examples of benign or refusal behaviors), with losses applied to reroute harmful representations and preserve benign ones. The approach will be implemented for both text-only and multimodal models, and extended to AI agents by controlling representations involved in function-calling and action selection.
ae16c93bf3a33c43e8f57293530069e77c89bcaa.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on state-of-the-art language models (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v2), multimodal models (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B), and AI agents with function-calling capabilities. Evaluation will use standardized benchmarks for harmfulness and robustness, such as HarmBench (covering a wide range of black-box and white-box adversarial attacks, including GCG, PAIR, TAP-Transfer, AutoDAN, multilingual, prefilling, input embedding, and representation-space attacks), as well as capability benchmarks like MTBench, OpenLLM Leaderboard, MMLU, ARC-c, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K, MMMU, LLaVA-Wild, and the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL). Baselines will include refusal-trained models, adversarially trained models (e.g., R2D2), and models with safety prompts. Attack success rates, compliance with harmful requests, and standard capability scores will be measured. Ablation studies will analyze the impact of dataset composition, loss functions, and representation layers.
ae16c93bf3a33c43e8f57293530069e77c89bcaa.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces a fundamentally new, attack-agnostic paradigm for AI safety by directly manipulating internal representations to prevent harmful outputs, rather than relying on input/output filtering or adversarial training. This approach generalizes across a wide range of unseen attacks, achieves high robustness with minimal or no loss in model utility, and can be applied to both language and multimodal models as well as AI agents. The framework demonstrates, for the first time, that the trade-off between harmlessness and capability can be significantly improved, advancing the Pareto frontier for robust alignment. The method also provides a practical and computationally efficient solution that does not require costly retraining or extensive adversarial data.

ae22db103c2954a56787a6c91373ea161841f250.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
ae22db103c2954a56787a6c91373ea161841f250.research_question: How do internal representations at different layers of large language models (LLMs) contribute to downstream task performance, and what underlying properties determine the quality of these representations across diverse architectures and domains?
ae22db103c2954a56787a6c91373ea161841f250.hypothesis: Intermediate layers of large language models encode richer and more robust representations than final layers, leading to improved performance on downstream tasks. The quality of these representations can be explained and quantified through unified metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance.
ae22db103c2954a56787a6c91373ea161841f250.proposed_method: A unified framework will be developed to analyze and quantify the quality of hidden representations at every layer of large language models. This framework will integrate information-theoretic metrics (such as matrix-based entropy and effective rank), geometric measures (such as curvature of token trajectories), and invariance-based metrics (such as InfoNCE, LiDAR, and DiME) to provide a comprehensive assessment of representation quality. The approach will involve computing these metrics layer-wise across multiple architectures, including transformer-based, state-space, and encoder-only models, as well as extending the analysis to vision models. Theoretical connections among these metrics will be established, and empirical studies will be conducted to correlate them with downstream task performance.
ae22db103c2954a56787a6c91373ea161841f250.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using a diverse set of model architectures, including decoder-only transformers (e.g., Pythia, Llama3), state-space models (e.g., Mamba), and encoder-based models (e.g., BERT, LLM2Vec). Each model will be evaluated layer-wise on 32 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), covering classification, clustering, and reranking tasks. Representation quality metrics will be computed for each layer using the WikiText-103 dataset and other standard benchmarks. Baselines will include final-layer embeddings and standard evaluation practices. Additional experiments will analyze the effects of model scale, training progression, fine-tuning (including chain-of-thought and supervised/unsupervised objectives), and input perturbations. Evaluation metrics will include downstream task accuracy, correlations between representation metrics and task performance, and robustness to input augmentations. Comparisons will also be made to vision models (e.g., ViT, CLIP, BEiT, DINOv2, MAE, AIM) to assess domain generality.
ae22db103c2954a56787a6c91373ea161841f250.novelty_claims: The proposed research introduces a unified theoretical and empirical framework that connects information-theoretic, geometric, and invariance-based metrics for assessing representation quality in neural networks. It systematically demonstrates that intermediate layers, rather than final layers, often provide superior features for downstream tasks across both language and vision domains. The approach challenges conventional reliance on final-layer representations and provides new diagnostic tools and insights for model design, training, and interpretability. The framework enables unsupervised selection of optimal layers and reveals how training objectives and architectural choices shape internal representations, offering practical implications for building more robust and accurate models.

ae31c2587bea859ea292eef09067185164b0c779.title: Optimal SQ Lower Bounds for Learning Halfspaces with Massart Noise
ae31c2587bea859ea292eef09067185164b0c779.research_question: What are the fundamental computational limits for efficiently learning halfspaces in the presence of Massart noise, specifically within the Statistical Query (SQ) framework, and how do these limits compare to information-theoretic optimality and existing algorithmic guarantees?
ae31c2587bea859ea292eef09067185164b0c779.hypothesis: Any SQ algorithm that achieves misclassification error better than the Massart noise parameter η for learning halfspaces requires either superpolynomially many queries or queries of superpolynomial accuracy, even when the information-theoretically optimal error is much smaller than η and an overwhelming fraction of examples are noiseless.
ae31c2587bea859ea292eef09067185164b0c779.proposed_method: A new lower bound construction will be developed for the problem of learning halfspaces under the Massart noise model in the SQ framework. The approach involves constructing two specific distributions over labeled examples such that their mixtures are SQ-hard to distinguish from a null distribution, even when the optimal error (OPT) is vanishingly small. The construction leverages moment-matching techniques, where two one-dimensional distributions (A and B) are carefully designed to match many moments of the standard Gaussian distribution and to satisfy the Massart noise condition with parameter η. The distributions are embedded into higher dimensions such that any degree-d polynomial threshold function (PTF) lower bound in lower dimensions yields a lower bound for halfspaces in higher dimensions. The reduction is carefully parameterized to ensure that the lower bound matches the upper bound achievable by known polynomial-time SQ algorithms.
ae31c2587bea859ea292eef09067185164b0c779.experiment_details: Theoretical experiments will be conducted by constructing distributions over high-dimensional spaces and analyzing the SQ complexity required to distinguish them. The analysis will involve quantifying the number and accuracy of SQ queries needed to achieve error better than η, as a function of the ambient dimension M and the noise parameter η. Theoretical baselines include known polynomial-time SQ algorithms for learning halfspaces under Massart noise, as well as previously established lower bounds for related noise models (e.g., random classification noise and agnostic learning). Evaluation metrics are the number of SQ queries and their accuracy required to achieve a given misclassification error. The setup also includes analysis for the Tsybakov noise model as a corollary, demonstrating hardness even as the fraction of noisy examples becomes vanishingly small.
ae31c2587bea859ea292eef09067185164b0c779.novelty_claims: The proposed approach establishes tight SQ lower bounds for learning halfspaces under Massart noise, matching the guarantees of the best known polynomial-time SQ algorithms and fully characterizing the efficiently achievable error in this setting. The construction demonstrates that achieving error better than η is SQ-hard even when the optimal error is much smaller and most examples are noiseless, closing the gap between previous lower bounds and algorithmic upper bounds. The method also extends to show SQ-hardness for the Tsybakov noise model, providing new insights into the computational hardness of learning under more general noise conditions. The technical innovation lies in a cleaner and more precise construction of hard distributions, enabling the tightest possible lower bound.

ae3d869719c15099889c02c03b922516b3b60aa0.title: How Good Are GPT Models at Machine Translation? A Comprehensive Evaluation
ae3d869719c15099889c02c03b922516b3b60aa0.research_question: How effective are large generative language models, specifically GPT models, at machine translation across a variety of language pairs, domains, and translation scenarios, and what are their strengths, limitations, and potential synergies with conventional neural machine translation systems?
ae3d869719c15099889c02c03b922516b3b60aa0.hypothesis: GPT models, when appropriately prompted and configured, can achieve competitive or superior machine translation quality compared to state-of-the-art research and commercial systems, particularly for high-resource languages and document-level tasks, and hybrid approaches combining GPT and NMT systems can further enhance translation performance.
ae3d869719c15099889c02c03b922516b3b60aa0.proposed_method: A comprehensive evaluation framework will be established to systematically assess the translation capabilities of several GPT models (e.g., text-davinci-002, text-davinci-003, ChatGPT) across 18 language pairs, including both high- and low-resource, English-centric and non-English-centric directions. The methodology will include zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies, with detailed investigation into prompt selection based on quality and relevance using sentence embeddings (e.g., LaBSE) and retrieval techniques. Both sentence-level and document-level translation scenarios will be explored, employing overlapping sliding window approaches for document context. Robustness to domain shift and the potential of hybrid GPT-NMT systems will be examined. Human evaluation and in-depth analysis of translation artifacts, language modeling biases, and output characteristics will be conducted to provide qualitative insights.
ae3d869719c15099889c02c03b922516b3b60aa0.experiment_details: Experiments will utilize publicly available datasets, primarily WMT22 test sets for most languages, with WMT21 for Icelandic and Hausa. Baselines will include top-ranked WMT research and commercial systems, as well as Microsoft Translator via Azure Cognitive Services. Evaluation metrics will comprise neural network-based metrics (COMET-22, COMETkiwi), lexical metrics (SacreBLEU, ChrF), and adapted document-level metrics (Doc-COMETkiwi, doc-BLEU). Both zero-shot and few-shot (1 and 5 shot) prompting will be tested, with prompt examples drawn from filtered WMT training data. Document-level translation will be evaluated using sliding window approaches to handle non-aligned outputs. Robustness will be assessed across four domains (Conversational, News, e-Commerce, Social), and human evaluation will be performed using contrastive Direct Assessment with professional annotators.
ae3d869719c15099889c02c03b922516b3b60aa0.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces the first large-scale, systematic evaluation of GPT models for machine translation across a diverse set of languages, domains, and translation scenarios, including both sentence- and document-level tasks. It proposes novel prompt selection strategies based on quality and relevance, adapts document-level evaluation metrics for large language model outputs, and investigates the hybridization of GPT and NMT systems. The work aims to provide new insights into the strengths, limitations, and distinctive translation behaviors of GPT models, as well as practical guidance for leveraging them in real-world translation applications.

ae67f0004ce9b2068cf7263b5ffc4089ac3fadb8.title: Do Vision & Language Decoders use Images and Text equally? How Self-consistent are their Explanations?
ae67f0004ce9b2068cf7263b5ffc4089ac3fadb8.research_question: To what extent do vision and language model (VLM) decoders utilize image and text modalities when generating answers and explanations, and how self-consistent are their explanations across different settings?
ae67f0004ce9b2068cf7263b5ffc4089ac3fadb8.hypothesis: VLM decoders rely more heavily on the text modality than the image modality when generating answers, but the image modality plays a more significant role during explanation generation, especially in chain-of-thought (CoT) settings. Furthermore, VLM decoders are less self-consistent in their explanations compared to large language models (LLMs).
ae67f0004ce9b2068cf7263b5ffc4089ac3fadb8.proposed_method: The proposed research will extend the MM-SHAP framework to autoregressive VLM decoders, enabling the quantification of modality contributions (image vs. text) for both answer and explanation generation. Shapley values will be computed for each input token (image patch or text token) across all output tokens, normalized, and aggregated to yield overall modality contributions. The CC-SHAP metric will be used to assess self-consistency by comparing the distributions of input token contributions when generating answers versus explanations, producing a continuous self-consistency score. Additionally, a suite of edit-based self-consistency tests (Counterfactual Edits, Biasing Features, Corrupting CoT) will be adapted to the multimodal setting to further probe model faithfulness and robustness.
ae67f0004ce9b2068cf7263b5ffc4089ac3fadb8.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on four state-of-the-art VLM decoders (BakLLaVA, LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral, LLaVA-NeXT-Vicuna, and mPLUG-Owl3), each with 7 billion parameters. The evaluation will utilize three generative datasets (VQA, GQA, GQAbalanced) for free-form answer generation and nine multiple-choice datasets (FoilIt!, MSCOCO, and the six instruments of the VALSE benchmark) for image-sentence alignment tasks. Baseline comparisons will include prior results from VL encoders and unimodal models. Evaluation metrics will comprise accuracy, caption precision, foil precision, pairwise accuracy, MM-SHAP modality contributions, and CC-SHAP self-consistency scores. Both post-hoc and CoT explanation settings will be tested, and experiments will be run on 100 random samples per dataset for computational tractability, with full VALSE results reported for all samples.
ae67f0004ce9b2068cf7263b5ffc4089ac3fadb8.novelty_claims: This research will provide the first systematic evaluation of the multimodal degree and self-consistency of state-of-the-art VLM decoders, extending MM-SHAP and CC-SHAP to autoregressive decoder architectures. The methodology will enable direct, accuracy-agnostic measurement of modality contributions and self-consistency in both answer and explanation generation, including the adaptation of language-only faithfulness tests to the multimodal domain. The research will also establish new benchmarking results for VLM decoders on the VALSE benchmark, previously focused on encoders, and offer insights into the relative importance of image and text modalities in current VLMs.

ae7606881a405a773dae6cce8efd87fe0b9b73d9.title: Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer
ae7606881a405a773dae6cce8efd87fe0b9b73d9.research_question: Can language models be effectively transferred to arbitrary new tokenizers without additional training, thereby increasing their flexibility and efficiency across languages and domains?
ae7606881a405a773dae6cce8efd87fe0b9b73d9.hypothesis: A hypernetwork trained to predict embedding parameters for arbitrary tokenizers can enable zero-shot transfer of language models to new tokenizers, preserving model performance and improving efficiency without the need for retraining.
ae7606881a405a773dae6cce8efd87fe0b9b73d9.proposed_method: A hypernetwork will be developed that takes as input a description of a new tokenizer (its vocabulary and tokenization function) and predicts the corresponding input and output embedding matrices for a pretrained language model. The hypernetwork will be trained on a diverse distribution of tokenizers, sampled by constructing UnigramLM tokenizers from rolling batches of text with added noise to encourage generalization. During training, a warmup stage will mimic the original model's embeddings, followed by a main stage minimizing the language modeling loss with the predicted embeddings, and an auxiliary loss to penalize drift from known embeddings. The hypernetwork architecture will use Transformer layers to compose the embeddings of decomposed tokens (from the original tokenizer) into new embeddings for the target tokenizer, amortizing over the tokenization function. Special procedures will be implemented to ensure compatibility between different tokenizer types (e.g., converting to byte-level or UnigramLM representations).
ae7606881a405a773dae6cce8efd87fe0b9b73d9.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on both encoder-style (e.g., XLM-R) and decoder-style (e.g., Mistral-7B) language models. The hypernetwork will be trained using the English subset of the MADLAD-400 corpus and StarCoder code data, with multilingual experiments using 26 languages from XGLM. Evaluation will include standard natural language benchmarks (PiQA, HellaSwag, BoolQ, MMLU, ARC), code synthesis (HumanEvalPack), and multilingual tasks (XNLI, XCOPA, multilingual MMLU). Baselines will include heuristic-based embedding initialization methods such as FOCUS, FVT, OFA, and lexical baselines. Metrics will include task accuracy, sequence length reduction, and inference speedup. Additional experiments will test continued training (n-shot transfer), transfer to fine-tuned models, and generalization to unseen languages and tokenizer types. Hypernetwork training will use a batch size of 128, sequence length of 128, and 200k training steps, with architecture and hyperparameters detailed for reproducibility.
ae7606881a405a773dae6cce8efd87fe0b9b73d9.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces the Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer (ZeTT) problem, defining and addressing the challenge of detaching language models from their original tokenizers. The proposed hypernetwork-based approach is novel in its ability to predict embeddings for arbitrary tokenizers in a zero-shot manner, generalizing across both encoder and decoder models. The method amortizes over the tokenization function and demonstrates robust performance across languages, domains, and even fine-tuned model variants. Empirical results claim substantial improvements over prior heuristics, significant reductions in sequence length and inference cost, and the ability to rapidly close any remaining performance gap with minimal continued training. The approach also provides new tools for combining models with different tokenizers and adapting to out-of-distribution vocabularies.

ae9a30ed24edab448cdb7a2e5269deb9713d2048.title: Memorization Through the Lens of Curvature of Loss Function Around Samples
ae9a30ed24edab448cdb7a2e5269deb9713d2048.research_question: How can the curvature of the loss function around individual training samples be leveraged to measure and understand memorization in deep neural networks, and what insights can this provide into dataset quality and failure modes?
ae9a30ed24edab448cdb7a2e5269deb9713d2048.hypothesis: The curvature of the loss function around a data sample, averaged over training epochs, serves as a reliable and scalable metric for quantifying the degree of memorization of that sample by a neural network.
ae9a30ed24edab448cdb7a2e5269deb9713d2048.proposed_method: A method will be developed to estimate the curvature of the loss function with respect to the input for each training sample in a deep neural network. Specifically, the trace of the square of the Hessian matrix of the loss with respect to the input will be computed using Hutchinson’s trace estimator, which involves averaging the squared norm of Hessian-vector products over several random Rademacher vectors. The curvature will be estimated efficiently using finite difference approximations and will be averaged over all training epochs to obtain a stable score for each sample. This approach avoids explicit computation of the full Hessian and is computationally scalable, requiring only a single network training run.
ae9a30ed24edab448cdb7a2e5269deb9713d2048.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on several popular image classification datasets, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet, using a ResNet18 architecture. Curvature scores will be computed for each training sample and analyzed both qualitatively (by visualizing high and low curvature samples) and quantitatively. Quantitative validation will involve comparing curvature-based memorization scores to established memorization baselines, such as Feldman & Zhang (2020) scores, using cosine similarity. Additional experiments will inject synthetic label noise (randomly corrupting a subset of labels) to test the method's ability to identify memorized, mislabeled samples, with performance measured by AUROC. Baselines for comparison will include inconfidence scores and Confident Learning (Cleanlab). Key experimental setups include training with and without weight decay and averaging curvature estimates over epochs.
ae9a30ed24edab448cdb7a2e5269deb9713d2048.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces a scalable, single-network method for measuring sample-level memorization via loss curvature, in contrast to prior methods requiring thousands of model retrainings. The method uncovers novel dataset failure modes, such as duplicated images with conflicting labels, that are not detected by existing memorization metrics. Additionally, the curvature-based metric demonstrates strong alignment with established memorization scores and outperforms alternative approaches in identifying mislabeled samples under synthetic corruption, while providing new insights into the dynamics of memorization and overfitting during training.

aec826ff336ca442697d5f908ab1668f1ea18987.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
aec826ff336ca442697d5f908ab1668f1ea18987.research_question: How do pre-trained language models internally implement basic mathematical operations, such as the greater-than comparison, and what are the mechanistic underpinnings of these abilities?
aec826ff336ca442697d5f908ab1668f1ea18987.hypothesis: Pre-trained language models, such as GPT-2 small, implement mathematical operations like greater-than through identifiable and interpretable computational circuits composed of specific attention heads and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), rather than through simple memorization or entirely generalized mechanisms.
aec826ff336ca442697d5f908ab1668f1ea18987.proposed_method: A mechanistic interpretability approach will be employed to uncover and analyze the internal circuits responsible for mathematical operations in GPT-2 small. The investigation will focus on a case study task—year-span prediction—where the model is prompted to predict valid end years greater than a given start year within a sentence. The methodology includes generating a controlled dataset of templated sentences, applying path patching (a causal intervention technique) to identify minimal subgraphs (circuits) in the model's computational graph that are sufficient and necessary for the greater-than operation, and analyzing the roles of individual components (attention heads and MLPs) within these circuits. Further, the internal representations and neuron-level contributions within the identified MLPs will be dissected using logit lens analysis and principal component analysis (PCA) to interpret how structured information is processed and composed.
aec826ff336ca442697d5f908ab1668f1ea18987.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using GPT-2 small, leveraging a dataset of 10,000 automatically generated year-span prediction examples, with nouns sampled from a curated pool and years selected to ensure valid tokenization. The model's output probabilities for candidate years will be evaluated using metrics such as probability difference (measuring preference for years greater than the start year) and cutoff sharpness (quantifying the output distribution's transition). Baseline model behavior will be compared to performance under various path patching interventions, including ablation and targeted input replacement, to validate the sufficiency and necessity of the identified circuits. Additional qualitative and quantitative analyses will be performed on related prompts to assess circuit generalization, and neuron-level interventions will be used to measure the distributed nature of the computation within MLPs.
aec826ff336ca442697d5f908ab1668f1ea18987.novelty_claims: The proposed research introduces a fine-grained mechanistic interpretability framework for uncovering and explaining the internal circuits responsible for mathematical reasoning in pre-trained language models. It advances the state of the art by moving beyond behavioral probes to causal, circuit-level explanations, and by demonstrating that mathematical operations like greater-than are implemented through complex, distributed interactions between attention heads and MLPs. The approach also provides new insights into the interplay between memorization and generalization in language model computations, and establishes methodologies that can be extended to other models and mathematical tasks.

aece4fa90c5d582c5d0e953d75c8a0cbae14d70e.title: Trainability enhancement of parameterized quantum circuits via reduced-domain parameter initialization
aece4fa90c5d582c5d0e953d75c8a0cbae14d70e.research_question: How can the trainability of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) be enhanced, particularly in the presence of barren plateaus and spurious local minima, through improved parameter initialization strategies?
aece4fa90c5d582c5d0e953d75c8a0cbae14d70e.hypothesis: Reducing the initial domain of each parameter in a PQC, inversely proportional to the square root of the circuit depth, will prevent the exponential decay of cost gradients and enhance trainability, thereby mitigating barren plateaus and reducing the occurrence of spurious local minima.
aece4fa90c5d582c5d0e953d75c8a0cbae14d70e.proposed_method: A novel parameter initialization strategy is developed wherein each variational parameter of a PQC is independently and uniformly sampled from a reduced interval [−aπ, aπ], with the hyperparameter 'a' scaling as Θ(1/√L), where L is the circuit depth. This approach is theoretically analyzed for variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) tasks, with rigorous proofs establishing lower bounds on the norm of the cost gradient and its variance under this initialization. The method is designed to be agnostic to the specific PQC topology and is applicable to Hamiltonians expressed as sums of local Pauli strings. During optimization, parameters are unconstrained and may leave the initial reduced domain as guided by the optimizer. Theoretical results are complemented by sensitivity analyses on the choice of 'a', and the strategy is further extended to quantum neural networks (QNNs) to address landscapes with exponentially many spurious local minima.
aece4fa90c5d582c5d0e953d75c8a0cbae14d70e.experiment_details: Experiments are conducted using classical simulations of VQE tasks for the N-qubit Heisenberg model, employing both hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA) and Hamiltonian variational ansatz (HVA) circuits. Multiple initialization strategies are compared, including zero-initialization, uniform initialization over [−π, π], Floquet initialization, Gaussian initialization, and the proposed reduced-domain initialization with theoretically derived 'a'. Evaluation metrics include the mean squared norm of the cost gradient at initialization, convergence of the cost function, and the average von Neumann entropy to assess entanglement. Experiments are performed across varying numbers of qubits and circuit depths, with additional robustness checks under finite measurement shot noise. For QNNs, hard training instances with exponentially many local minima are used to compare the probability of global convergence under different initializations, with thousands of random trials per setting.
aece4fa90c5d582c5d0e953d75c8a0cbae14d70e.novelty_claims: The proposed reduced-domain parameter initialization strategy is claimed to provide the first theoretical guarantee that the magnitude of the cost gradient decays at most polynomially with respect to qubit count and circuit depth, as opposed to the exponential decay observed with standard initializations. The method is shown to enhance trainability and convergence in both VQE and QNN contexts, and to protect against exponentially many spurious local minima. The approach is general, applicable to a wide range of PQC architectures and Hamiltonians, and is supported by both rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive numerical simulations. This work offers new insights into balancing trainability and expressibility in variational quantum algorithms through principled parameter initialization.

aecfd9aa63450629aafae9595c33ed325c0c8f29.title: MATES: Model-Aware Data Selection for Efficient Pretraining with Data Influence Models
aecfd9aa63450629aafae9595c33ed325c0c8f29.research_question: How can pretraining data be dynamically selected to maximize language model pretraining efficiency and downstream performance, by accounting for the evolving data preferences of the model during training?
aecfd9aa63450629aafae9595c33ed325c0c8f29.hypothesis: Continuously adapting data selection to the evolving preferences of the pretraining model, using a model-aware data influence estimation, will yield more efficient pretraining and improved downstream task performance compared to static or heuristic-based data selection methods.
aecfd9aa63450629aafae9595c33ed325c0c8f29.proposed_method: A model-aware data selection framework will be developed, where a small data influence model is trained to predict the influence of each data point on the target performance of the pretraining model. At each stage of pretraining, the current language model will be locally probed to estimate the oracle data influence by measuring the change in reference loss after a one-step update with individual data points. These oracle influence scores will be used to fine-tune the data influence model, which then predicts influence scores for the entire pretraining corpus. The most influential data points will be selected for the next pretraining stage using a Gumbel-Top-k sampling strategy weighted by predicted influence. This process will be repeated periodically, ensuring that data selection is continuously aligned with the model's evolving data needs.
aecfd9aa63450629aafae9595c33ed325c0c8f29.experiment_details: Experiments will involve pretraining language models of 410M and 1B parameters from scratch using the Pythia architecture on the C4 dataset. The data influence model will be instantiated as a BERT-base model, fine-tuned on locally probed oracle data influence scores. At each pretraining stage (every 10k steps), 20% of the data will be sampled based on influence scores, with LAMBADA serving as the primary reference task for influence estimation. Evaluation will be conducted using the lm-evaluation-harness on nine diverse downstream tasks (including SciQ, ARC-E, ARC-C, LogiQA, OBQA, BoolQ, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande), reporting zero-shot accuracy and total GPU FLOPs. Baselines will include random selection, rule-based filtering, deduplication, proximity-based, static influence-function-based, and LLM-based data selection methods.
aecfd9aa63450629aafae9595c33ed325c0c8f29.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces a dynamic, model-aware data selection framework that continuously adapts to the evolving data preferences of the pretraining model. It leverages a small, efficiently updated data influence model to approximate oracle influence, enabling on-the-fly selection of the most effective pretraining data. This method is claimed to significantly improve pretraining efficiency, reduce computational cost (FLOPs), and outperform both static and state-of-the-art data selection baselines, including those relying on much larger reference models. The approach also demonstrates robust generalization across tasks and provides insights into the changing nature of model data preferences during pretraining.

aed9fd4f7c29001baaa3030a0f8fd20bd8713c2f.title: Statistical Guarantees for Variational Autoencoders using PAC-Bayesian Theory
aed9fd4f7c29001baaa3030a0f8fd20bd8713c2f.research_question: How can rigorous statistical generalization guarantees be established for variational autoencoders (VAEs), particularly regarding their reconstruction, regeneration, and generative properties?
aed9fd4f7c29001baaa3030a0f8fd20bd8713c2f.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that PAC-Bayesian theory can be leveraged to derive meaningful, non-vacuous generalization bounds for VAEs, providing statistical guarantees for their reconstruction loss and the Wasserstein distance between the data-generating and generated distributions.
aed9fd4f7c29001baaa3030a0f8fd20bd8713c2f.proposed_method: A new theoretical framework will be developed that applies PAC-Bayesian theory to the analysis of VAEs. The approach will start by deriving a novel PAC-Bayesian bound for conditional posterior distributions, specifically tailored to the variational posterior used in VAEs. This bound will be applied to the VAE setting by treating the latent space as the hypothesis class, aligning the VAE's prior and posterior with the PAC-Bayesian prior and posterior. The methodology will establish generalization bounds for the VAE's reconstruction loss, as well as upper bounds on the Wasserstein distance between the input distribution and both the regenerated and generated distributions. The analysis will consider both bounded instance spaces and the manifold hypothesis, with explicit dependence on the Lipschitz constants of the encoder and decoder networks and the empirical VAE objective components.
aed9fd4f7c29001baaa3030a0f8fd20bd8713c2f.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on synthetic datasets to empirically validate the derived PAC-Bayesian bounds. The evaluation will focus on the VAE's reconstruction loss and the Wasserstein distance between the true data distribution and the VAE's generated and regenerated distributions. Baseline comparisons will include standard VAE training objectives, while the proposed method's certificates will be computed using held-out samples distinct from those used for training. Evaluation metrics will include empirical reconstruction loss (RMSE), KL divergence, and Wasserstein distance, with attention to how these quantities relate to the theoretical upper bounds. The experimental setup will also consider the effects of different choices of reconstruction loss and the impact of the manifold assumption on the tightness of the bounds.
aed9fd4f7c29001baaa3030a0f8fd20bd8713c2f.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces the first PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for VAEs that directly address conditional posteriors, enabling statistical guarantees for both reconstruction and generative performance. The framework provides the first upper bounds on the Wasserstein distance between the data-generating distribution and the VAE's generative model, as well as the regenerated distribution.
