The approach consists of three main components: (1) a domain adapter, implemented via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), is first trained to bridge the visual quality gap between high-quality image datasets and lower-quality video datasets; (2) a temporal Transformer-based motion module is then inserted and trained on video data to distill transferable motion priors, with the image layers of the base model kept frozen to preserve content priors; (3) an optional MotionLoRA module enables efficient adaptation of the pre-trained motion module to new motion patterns using a small set of reference videos and minimal training iterations. The entire pipeline is designed for plug-and-play integration, allowing the motion module and MotionLoRA to be inserted into any personalized T2I model derived from the same base.
c1caa303549764d220ff17dc1785985dd1ba6047.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using Stable Diffusion v1.5 as the base model, with the motion module trained on the WebVid-10M video dataset. Evaluation will utilize a diverse set of personalized T2I models sourced from community platforms such as Civitai and HuggingFace, covering a broad range of visual domains. Baseline comparisons will include recent video generation methods (e.g., Text2Video-Zero, Tune-a-Video) and commercial tools (Gen-2, PikaLabs). Evaluation metrics will include both user studies (measuring text alignment, domain similarity, and motion smoothness via average user ranking) and automated CLIP-based metrics. Ablation studies will assess the impact of the domain adapter and the efficiency of MotionLoRA in terms of parameter and data requirements.
c1caa303549764d220ff17dc1785985dd1ba6047.novelty_claims: The proposed framework enables animation generation for any personalized text-to-image diffusion model without requiring model-specific fine-tuning, significantly reducing computational and data costs. The introduction of a plug-and-play motion module trained once and transferable across models is novel, as is the MotionLoRA technique for efficient motion pattern adaptation with minimal data and storage overhead. The approach preserves the visual quality and domain knowledge of the original personalized models and is compatible with existing content-controlling techniques, enabling controllable animation generation without additional training.

c1d654386de0cee2561001e2de2ad444430323d1.title: SLAB: Efficient Transformers with Simplified Linear Attention and Progressive Re-parameterized Batch Normalization
c1d654386de0cee2561001e2de2ad444430323d1.research_question: How can transformer architectures be made more computationally efficient for deployment on resource-constrained devices, without sacrificing accuracy, by addressing bottlenecks in normalization layers and attention modules?
c1d654386de0cee2561001e2de2ad444430323d1.hypothesis: Progressively replacing LayerNorm with a re-parameterized BatchNorm during training, combined with a simplified linear attention mechanism, will enable transformer models to achieve comparable or superior accuracy with significantly reduced inference latency and computational cost.
c1d654386de0cee2561001e2de2ad444430323d1.proposed_method: The proposed approach introduces a progressive normalization strategy where LayerNorm is gradually replaced by a re-parameterized BatchNorm (RepBN) during training. This transition is controlled by a hyper-parameter that decays over training steps, ensuring stable convergence and mitigating the risk of training collapse. The RepBN formulation allows for end-to-end learning and can be re-parameterized to a standard BatchNorm for efficient inference, enabling fusion with adjacent linear layers. Additionally, a Simplified Linear Attention (SLA) module is developed, which employs ReLU as the kernel function and incorporates a depth-wise convolution for local feature enhancement. This attention mechanism decouples the computation order to achieve linear complexity with respect to sequence length, further reducing computational burden while maintaining high representational capacity.
c1d654386de0cee2561001e2de2ad444430323d1.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on a range of computer vision and language modeling tasks. For image classification, models will be trained on ImageNet-1K using standard protocols (300 epochs, AdamW optimizer, cosine learning rate decay, batch size 1024, and 224x224 image resolution), with throughput and latency measured on a V100 GPU. Object detection and instance segmentation will be evaluated using Mask R-CNN on the COCO dataset, with various transformer backbones pretrained on ImageNet-1K and latency measured per batch. For language modeling, experiments will utilize the Wikitext-103 dataset and the LLaMA-350M model, with perplexity and throughput as primary metrics. Baselines will include standard LayerNorm-based transformers, BatchNorm-based variants, and recent efficient transformer designs such as Flatten Transformer. Evaluation metrics will include top-1 accuracy for classification, mAP for detection/segmentation, perplexity for language modeling, and inference latency/throughput for all tasks.
c1d654386de0cee2561001e2de2ad444430323d1.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces a progressive normalization strategy that enables stable training and efficient inference by transitioning from LayerNorm to a re-parameterized BatchNorm, which can be fused with linear layers for hardware-friendly deployment. The simplified linear attention module offers a computationally efficient alternative to existing linear attention mechanisms, leveraging ReLU and depth-wise convolution for strong performance. The combination of these techniques achieves state-of-the-art trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency across multiple tasks and architectures, providing a practical solution for deploying transformers on resource-constrained devices.

c1e384e3e1d9015aea7a5f1cb0b4ecc5b59fdca6.title: Learning Linear Attention in Polynomial Time
c1e384e3e1d9015aea7a5f1cb0b4ecc5b59fdca6.research_question: Can multi-head linear attention networks be efficiently learned from arbitrary datasets in polynomial time, and under what conditions can their learned representations be certified to generalize out-of-distribution?
c1e384e3e1d9015aea7a5f1cb0b4ecc5b59fdca6.hypothesis: Single-layer multi-head linear attention networks are strongly, agnostically PAC-learnable in polynomial time, and there exists a data-dependent, efficiently checkable condition that certifies all empirical risk minimizers compute the same function, ensuring robust generalization.
c1e384e3e1d9015aea7a5f1cb0b4ecc5b59fdca6.proposed_method: A polynomial-time algorithm is developed to learn the optimal parameters of a multi-head linear attention (MHLA) network for any given dataset. The approach reformulates the learning of MHLA as a regression problem in a suitably defined reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) by constructing a cubic polynomial feature map from the input data. The algorithm first extracts these features, then solves a least-squares regression to find an optimal matrix W, and finally applies singular value decomposition (SVD) to recover the MHLA parameters (value and key-query matrices) with at most d^2 heads. Additionally, a certifiable identifiability criterion is introduced: by computing the minimum eigenvalue of the second-moment matrix of the feature map, it is possible to efficiently check whether all empirical risk minimizers are functionally equivalent on all inputs.
c1e384e3e1d9015aea7a5f1cb0b4ecc5b59fdca6.experiment_details: Experiments are conducted on synthetic datasets generated by single-layer linear attention networks, key–value associative memory tasks, and learning to execute finite automata. Models are trained using both the proposed regression-based algorithm and stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Baselines include single-head and multi-layer linear attention networks, as well as standard Transformer models with softmax attention. Evaluation metrics include training and validation loss, convergence speed, and distance in feature space to ground truth parameters. The effect of over-parameterization (number of heads vs. number of layers) is systematically studied, and the certifiable identifiability criterion is empirically validated by correlating the minimum eigenvalue of the data covariance matrix with generalization error and parameter recovery.
c1e384e3e1d9015aea7a5f1cb0b4ecc5b59fdca6.novelty_claims: This proposal introduces the first polynomial-time, strong agnostic PAC-learning result for single-layer multi-head linear attention networks, bridging the gap between expressivity and learnability. It provides a novel reduction of MHLA learning to kernel regression, enabling efficient global optimization and parameter recovery. The certifiable identifiability criterion offers a new, data-dependent, efficiently checkable guarantee for out-of-distribution generalization. Empirical studies reveal that over-parameterization by increasing the number of heads, rather than layers, significantly improves optimization and generalization, aligning with the theoretical findings.

c1fa6255cc9fc3128f74befc7855e255bc7a2c6e.title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
c1fa6255cc9fc3128f74befc7855e255bc7a2c6e.research_question: How can memory efficiency be improved during the training and fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) without sacrificing model performance, particularly on hardware with limited memory resources?
c1fa6255cc9fc3128f74befc7855e255bc7a2c6e.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that projecting gradients into a low-rank subspace during training can significantly reduce optimizer state memory usage while maintaining or improving model performance compared to existing low-rank adaptation methods.
c1fa6255cc9fc3128f74befc7855e255bc7a2c6e.proposed_method: A novel training strategy, Gradient Low-Rank Projection (GaLore), will be developed to enable full-parameter learning while reducing memory consumption. The method will periodically compute projection matrices (P and Q) via singular value decomposition (SVD) of the gradient matrix, projecting the gradient into a low-rank subspace before applying optimizer updates (e.g., Adam, Adafactor). Only the low-rank projected gradients and their statistics will be stored, drastically reducing the memory required for optimizer states. The projection subspace will be updated at a configurable frequency to adapt to changes in the gradient's principal directions, ensuring full-rank learning over time. GaLore will be designed to be optimizer-agnostic and compatible with quantized optimizers (e.g., 8-bit Adam) and per-layer weight updates for further memory savings.
c1fa6255cc9fc3128f74befc7855e255bc7a2c6e.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on both pre-training and fine-tuning tasks. For pre-training, LLaMA-based architectures (1B and 7B parameters) will be trained on the C4 dataset with up to 19.7B tokens, using BF16 and 8-bit precision formats. Baselines will include full-rank training, LoRA, ReLoRA, and traditional low-rank factorization approaches, with all methods tuned for comparable computational budgets. Evaluation metrics will include validation perplexity and actual memory usage (parameters plus optimizer states), measured on both data center GPUs (A100) and consumer GPUs (RTX 4090) without activation checkpointing or memory offloading. For fine-tuning, RoBERTa-Base will be evaluated on GLUE benchmark tasks, comparing GaLore to full fine-tuning and LoRA using average task scores and memory consumption. Ablation studies will investigate the effects of subspace rank and switching frequency on convergence and memory trade-offs.
c1fa6255cc9fc3128f74befc7855e255bc7a2c6e.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces a memory-efficient training framework that leverages the natural low-rank structure of gradients, rather than weights, to reduce optimizer state memory by up to 65.5% (and up to 82.5% with quantized optimizers), while maintaining or surpassing the performance of full-rank and existing low-rank methods. GaLore is the first method to demonstrate feasible pre-training of a 7B parameter LLM on a single 24GB consumer GPU without model parallelism, checkpointing, or offloading. The method is optimizer-agnostic, easy to integrate, and compatible with other memory-saving techniques, representing a significant advancement in scalable, resource-efficient LLM training.

c1fca46e51ef3f9e49877ccb75fc31fd70bc60e7.title: GAP: Differentially Private Graph Neural Networks with Aggregation Perturbation
c1fca46e51ef3f9e49877ccb75fc31fd70bc60e7.research_question: How can graph neural networks be trained and deployed with formal differential privacy guarantees, protecting sensitive information in both the graph structure (edges) and node attributes, while maintaining high utility for node classification tasks?
c1fca46e51ef3f9e49877ccb75fc31fd70bc60e7.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that a modular graph neural network architecture, which perturbs the aggregation function with calibrated noise and decouples feature encoding from graph-based aggregation, can achieve strong differential privacy guarantees at both edge and node levels, including during inference, while preserving much of the predictive accuracy compared to non-private and existing private baselines.
c1fca46e51ef3f9e49877ccb75fc31fd70bc60e7.proposed_method: A novel framework, GAP (Graph neural network with Aggregation Perturbation), is developed to provide differentially private learning and inference for GNNs. The architecture is composed of three modules: (i) an encoder module that pre-trains a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on node features and labels to produce low-dimensional node embeddings without using the graph structure; (ii) an aggregation module that recursively computes multi-hop node aggregations using the adjacency matrix, adding calibrated Gaussian noise to each aggregation step to ensure privacy, followed by normalization of the aggregated vectors; and (iii) a classification module that takes the set of private, cached aggregations and predicts node labels using a neural network, without further querying the graph. The method supports both edge-level and node-level privacy: for node-level privacy, the encoder and classifier are trained with DP-SGD, and neighbor sampling is used to bound node degree. The modular design ensures that privacy costs do not accumulate with training iterations, and inference privacy is guaranteed without additional privacy budget.
c1fca46e51ef3f9e49877ccb75fc31fd70bc60e7.experiment_details: Experiments are conducted on three real-world graph datasets of varying scale: Facebook (social network), Reddit (social posts), and Amazon (product co-purchasing), each with thousands to millions of nodes and edges. The proposed method is compared against state-of-the-art differentially private GNN baselines (e.g., graph perturbation with GraphSAGE, DP-SGD-based GNNs) and non-private models, as well as MLP baselines that do not use graph structure. Both edge-level and node-level privacy settings are evaluated, with privacy accounting performed using the Analytical Moments Accountant and privacy budgets (epsilon) varied across a range of values. Evaluation metrics include node classification accuracy, and experiments are repeated with multiple random splits and hyperparameter sweeps. The setup includes careful calibration of noise scales, use of neighbor sampling for bounded degree, and both transductive and inductive inference scenarios.
c1fca46e51ef3f9e49877ccb75fc31fd70bc60e7.novelty_claims: The proposed approach is the first to provide both edge-level and node-level differential privacy guarantees for GNNs in a unified framework, supporting multi-hop aggregation and inference privacy without additional privacy cost. The method introduces a modular architecture that decouples feature encoding from aggregation, enabling significant reductions in privacy budget consumption and improved utility compared to prior work. The aggregation perturbation mechanism allows for efficient, private multi-hop neighborhood aggregation, and the design ensures that privacy guarantees hold for both training and inference. Empirical results demonstrate superior accuracy-privacy trade-offs over existing private GNN methods and MLP baselines.

c2260403fd5cb2de73491323433e48b6ec36872c.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: a Theoretical Perspective
c2260403fd5cb2de73491323433e48b6ec36872c.research_question: What are the fundamental mechanisms that enable Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to enhance the reasoning and problem-solving abilities of large language models, particularly in mathematical and decision-making tasks, and what are the expressivity limits of Transformers with and without CoT?
c2260403fd5cb2de73491323433e48b6ec36872c.hypothesis: Equipping autoregressive Transformers with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation enables them to efficiently solve complex mathematical and decision-making problems that are otherwise intractable for bounded-depth Transformers without CoT, unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to input length.
c2260403fd5cb2de73491323433e48b6ec36872c.proposed_method: A theoretical and empirical investigation will be conducted into the expressivity of autoregressive Transformers with and without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation. The approach will leverage circuit complexity theory to establish lower and upper bounds on the model size required to solve arithmetic expression evaluation, linear equation solving, and dynamic programming (DP) problems. Explicit constructions of constant-size autoregressive Transformers capable of generating step-by-step CoT solutions in a formalized math language will be developed. The method will also analyze the recursive nature of CoT, which effectively increases the computational depth of the model through iterative output-feedback, and will generalize the analysis to a broad class of DP problems by formalizing their state space, transition, and aggregation functions.
c2260403fd5cb2de73491323433e48b6ec36872c.experiment_details: Experiments will be performed on four tasks: arithmetic expression evaluation, linear equation solving, longest increasing subsequence (LIS), and edit distance (ED). For each task, datasets will be constructed with varying levels of difficulty (e.g., increasing number of operators, variables, or sequence lengths), with 1 million samples for training and 0.1 million for testing, ensuring no overlap. Two training regimes will be compared: models trained to directly predict answers and models trained with full CoT demonstrations (including intermediate reasoning steps). Standard Transformer architectures with fixed hidden dimension and number of heads will be trained using the AdamW optimizer, and accuracy will be reported as the main evaluation metric. Additional experiments will assess robustness to corrupted or incomplete CoT data and the ability to generalize to longer input sequences than seen during training.
c2260403fd5cb2de73491323433e48b6ec36872c.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces a rigorous theoretical framework that explains why CoT dramatically enhances the expressivity of Transformers, showing that constant-size autoregressive models can solve complex reasoning tasks via step-by-step derivations, while direct answer prediction is provably intractable for bounded-depth models. The approach leverages circuit complexity theory to establish both impossibility and constructive results, and extends the analysis to general dynamic programming problems. The empirical component demonstrates, for the first time, that Transformers trained with CoT not only achieve near-perfect accuracy on challenging reasoning tasks but also exhibit robustness to data corruption and strong generalization to longer sequences. This work provides foundational insights into the mechanisms underlying CoT and its critical role in unlocking the reasoning capabilities of large language models.

c226a4acb42912054d498bcf771023b0ba2da001.title: Language Model Self-improvement by Reinforcement Learning Contemplation
c226a4acb42912054d498bcf771023b0ba2da001.research_question: Can large language models be improved in an unsupervised manner by leveraging their own self-evaluation capabilities, without relying on external labels or human feedback, across a variety of natural language processing tasks such as reasoning, text generation, and machine translation?
c226a4acb42912054d498bcf771023b0ba2da001.hypothesis: Large language models possess sufficient self-evaluation ability to serve as both student and teacher, enabling effective self-improvement through reinforcement learning using self-generated evaluation as reward, thereby enhancing performance on diverse NLP tasks without external supervision.
c226a4acb42912054d498bcf771023b0ba2da001.proposed_method: A novel framework, termed Self-Improvement by Reinforcement Learning Contemplation (SIRLC), is proposed for unsupervised fine-tuning of large language models. The method assigns the language model dual roles: as a student, it generates answers to unlabeled questions; as a teacher, it evaluates the quality or correctness of its own generated answers using specific evaluation prompts. The evaluation output is converted into a numerical reward (either binary or on a scale, depending on the task) via a text processing function. The model is then updated using reinforcement learning, specifically Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), to maximize the self-evaluation reward. Entropy regularization and KL-divergence constraints are applied to ensure stable training and prevent the model from diverging excessively from the initial pre-trained state. The self-evaluation model is kept fixed during training to maintain reward stability.
c226a4acb42912054d498bcf771023b0ba2da001.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on a range of NLP tasks divided into three categories: reasoning (using 12 challenging tasks from the BigBench-hard benchmark), language translation (IWSLT2017 dataset), and text summarization (CNN/DailyMail and BBC datasets). Baseline methods for comparison include Self-Consistency (SC), LMSI (self-consistency-based self-training), Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning (RLFT) with oracle metrics, and direct generation (DG) without self-evaluation. Evaluation metrics will include answer accuracy for reasoning tasks and BERTScore, BLEU, and ROUGE for translation and summarization. Training will use PPO for 6,000 gradient steps per task, with batch sizes of 12, and results will be averaged over three random seeds. The method will be tested on models of varying sizes (80M, 250M, 780M parameters) and its generalization to unseen datasets will be assessed by training on a subset of tasks and evaluating on others.
c226a4acb42912054d498bcf771023b0ba2da001.novelty_claims: The proposed approach eliminates the need for external supervision or reward models by leveraging the language model's own self-evaluation ability as the reward signal in reinforcement learning. This is claimed to be the first formal verification and application of LLM self-evaluation for unsupervised self-improvement across a broad range of NLP tasks. The method demonstrates effectiveness across diverse tasks, model sizes, and shows generalization to unseen datasets, establishing its broad applicability and scalability.

c259e512ced41063c3c032a6f9ebcabc63986cda.title: PMR: Prototypical Modal Rebalance for Multimodal Learning
c259e512ced41063c3c032a6f9ebcabc63986cda.research_question: How can the performance of multimodal learning systems be improved by addressing the modality imbalance problem, where dominant modalities suppress the learning of weaker modalities, in a way that is independent of specific model architectures and fusion strategies?
c259e512ced41063c3c032a6f9ebcabc63986cda.hypothesis: Introducing a prototypical modality rebalance strategy that actively accelerates the learning of slow-learning modalities and alleviates suppression from dominant modalities will improve overall multimodal learning performance and enable each modality to better exploit its features, regardless of the underlying fusion method or model structure.
c259e512ced41063c3c032a6f9ebcabc63986cda.proposed_method: A novel framework, Prototypical Modal Rebalance (PMR), is developed to address modality imbalance in multimodal learning. The method introduces class prototypes—centroids of each class in the representation space—for each modality, which are used to construct non-parametric classifiers for uni-modal performance evaluation. A prototypical cross-entropy (PCE) loss is applied to actively accelerate the slow-learning modality by enhancing its clustering toward the prototypes, while a prototype-based entropy regularization (PER) term is introduced during early training to slow down the convergence of the dominant modality and prevent premature suppression. The approach dynamically monitors the imbalance between modalities using a prototype-based metric and adjusts the learning pace of each modality accordingly. The method operates solely on modality representations, making it agnostic to the underlying model architecture and fusion strategy, and computes prototypes in a momentum fashion using a subset of training data.
c259e512ced41063c3c032a6f9ebcabc63986cda.experiment_details: Experiments are proposed on three multimodal datasets: CREMA-D (audio-visual emotion recognition), AVE (audio-visual event localization), and Colored-and-gray MNIST (synthetic multimodal classification). The evaluation will use several fusion methods, including concatenation, summation, film, and gated, as well as intermediate fusion architectures like MMTM and CentralNet. Baselines will include vanilla fusion methods, uni-modal models, and state-of-the-art modality imbalance mitigation techniques such as Modality-Drop, Gradient-Blending, and OGM-GE. Performance will be measured using classification accuracy and event localization accuracy, with additional analysis of uni-modal branch performance and imbalance ratio metrics. Ablation studies will assess the impact of subset size for prototype computation and compatibility with different optimizers (SGD, AdaGrad, Adam).
c259e512ced41063c3c032a6f9ebcabc63986cda.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces a modality-agnostic, architecture-independent strategy for addressing modality imbalance in multimodal learning by leveraging non-parametric, prototype-based losses and regularization. Unlike prior approaches, PMR does not require additional model structures or reliance on specific fusion methods, and it actively encourages the slow-learning modality to improve, rather than passively reducing the influence of the dominant modality. The approach is claimed to be generalizable across a wide range of tasks, datasets, and fusion strategies, and demonstrates consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

c26bb68806a992bf4fc85b5639e1657a445c4781.title: On the Representation Collapse of Sparse Mixture of Experts
c26bb68806a992bf4fc85b5639e1657a445c4781.research_question: How can the representation collapse issue in sparse mixture-of-experts (SMoE) models be alleviated to improve model capacity utilization and routing consistency, particularly in large-scale language model pre-training and downstream cross-lingual tasks?
c26bb68806a992bf4fc85b5639e1657a445c4781.hypothesis: Estimating routing scores between tokens and experts on a low-dimensional hypersphere, combined with dimension reduction, L2 normalization, and a learnable gating temperature, will alleviate representation collapse in SMoE models, resulting in improved model performance and more consistent routing behaviors.
c26bb68806a992bf4fc85b5639e1657a445c4781.proposed_method: A novel routing algorithm for SMoE models is proposed, which projects token hidden representations and expert embeddings into a shared low-dimensional space using a linear projection. Both token and expert vectors are then L2-normalized, so that routing scores are computed as cosine similarities on a unit hypersphere, mitigating the effect of expert embedding norms and encouraging more uniform and expressive representations. A learnable temperature parameter is incorporated into the gating function (softmax or sigmoid) to control the sharpness of expert activation, compensating for the normalization-induced score range. The method also includes a load balancing loss to ensure equitable expert utilization, and during fine-tuning, the router and expert parameters are frozen to prevent overfitting and maintain routing consistency.
c26bb68806a992bf4fc85b5639e1657a445c4781.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on cross-lingual language model pre-training using a combination of CCNet and Wikipedia corpora, sampling sentences from 94 languages with a re-balanced distribution to emphasize low-resource languages. The model backbone is a Transformer encoder (L=12, H=768, A=12), with a 32-expert sparse layer inserted after the 6th Transformer block. Baselines include a dense Transformer and a Switch Transformer-based SMoE with both softmax and sigmoid gating. Evaluation will be performed on seven XTREME cross-lingual benchmarks (POS, NER, XQuAD, MLQA, TyDiQA, XNLI, PAWS-X) using metrics such as F1, EM, and accuracy, as well as on multilingual machine translation (WMT-10, BLEU scores) and masked language modeling (validation perplexity). Ablation studies will assess the impact of dimension reduction, normalization, and routing freezing, and additional analyses will measure representation collapse and routing consistency.
c26bb68806a992bf4fc85b5639e1657a445c4781.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces a new routing algorithm for SMoE models that estimates routing scores on a low-dimensional hypersphere, directly addressing the under-explored issue of representation collapse in sparse expert architectures. Key innovations include the combination of dimension reduction, L2 normalization, and a learnable gating temperature, as well as the strategy of freezing routing during fine-tuning for improved consistency. The method claims consistent performance gains over existing SMoE and dense baselines across multiple multilingual tasks, and provides comprehensive analyses demonstrating improved representation diversity and routing stability.

c275a595e4370bc1454d1b51595e793707b0ddbc.title: Simulated Annealing in Early Layers Leads to Better Generalization
c275a595e4370bc1454d1b51595e793707b0ddbc.research_question: How can iterative training strategies be improved to enhance generalization and transferability of deep neural networks, particularly by modifying the optimization dynamics in early layers?
c275a595e4370bc1454d1b51595e793707b0ddbc.hypothesis: Applying simulated annealing-inspired gradient ascent phases specifically to the early layers of a neural network during iterative training will promote the learning of more generalizable and transferable features, outperforming existing methods such as later-layer-forgetting (LLF) and standard training.
c275a595e4370bc1454d1b51595e793707b0ddbc.proposed_method: A new iterative training framework is developed in which the neural network is partitioned into early (forgetting) and later (fit) layers using a layer threshold. At the start of each generation, a short phase of gradient ascent is performed exclusively on the early layers (forgetting hypothesis) for a fixed number of epochs, with a reduced learning rate to prevent divergence. Simultaneously, the later layers (fit hypothesis) are trained with standard gradient descent. After this ascent phase, both early and later layers continue with standard gradient descent for the remainder of the generation. The ascent learning rate is scaled down by a factor (e.g., S = 0.01) relative to the standard learning rate to ensure stability. Weight decay is adjusted for the ascent phase to avoid increasing the norm of the weights. This process is repeated for multiple generations, without re-initializing any layers, in contrast to LLF.
c275a595e4370bc1454d1b51595e793707b0ddbc.experiment_details: Experiments are conducted using the Tiny-ImageNet dataset for primary training and evaluation, employing a ResNet-50 backbone trained with SGD (momentum 0.9, weight decay 5e-4), cosine learning rate decay, and standard data augmentations. The method is compared against baselines including standard training (short and long), and LLF, using identical optimization settings and layer thresholds. Transfer learning performance is evaluated by linear probing on multiple downstream datasets (Flower, CUB, Aircraft, MIT, Stanford Dogs), and few-shot transfer is assessed using the Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning (CD-FSL) benchmark, with both linear and affine parameter fine-tuning. Evaluation metrics include classification accuracy, prediction depth (via k-NN probes at each layer), and analysis of Hessian eigenvalues to assess minima sharpness and robustness. All results are averaged over multiple runs and episodes, with detailed ablation studies on the effect of ascent phases and layer partitioning.
c275a595e4370bc1454d1b51595e793707b0ddbc.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces a novel use of simulated annealing-inspired gradient ascent phases restricted to early layers during iterative training, rather than re-initialization or perturbation of later layers. This method is claimed to yield superior generalization, deeper and more robust prediction depth, and significantly improved transfer and few-shot learning performance compared to state-of-the-art iterative training methods such as LLF. Additional contributions include empirical evidence of flatter minima (via Hessian analysis) and ablation studies demonstrating the critical role of early-layer annealing in achieving these gains.

c28e95a06dfcf13fc65a1cac83722f53e34f12a5.title: Autoformalization with Large Language Models
c28e95a06dfcf13fc65a1cac83722f53e34f12a5.research_question: Can large language models be leveraged to automatically translate natural language mathematical statements into formal specifications and proofs, and can these autoformalized statements be used to improve neural theorem provers?
c28e95a06dfcf13fc65a1cac83722f53e34f12a5.hypothesis: Large language models possess sufficient linguistic and mathematical reasoning capabilities to autoformalize a significant portion of mathematical problems, and the resulting formalized statements can be used to enhance the performance of neural theorem provers through additional training.
c28e95a06dfcf13fc65a1cac83722f53e34f12a5.proposed_method: A framework will be developed that utilizes large language models (LLMs), such as PaLM and Codex, to perform autoformalization of natural language mathematical statements into formal code for interactive theorem provers like Isabelle/HOL. The method will employ in-context learning by providing a few-shot prompt consisting of example translations from natural language to formal statements. The LLMs will be tasked with translating new mathematical competition problems, and their outputs will be evaluated for syntactic and semantic correctness. The autoformalized statements will then be used as new training data for a neural theorem prover, which will be iteratively improved using an expert iteration approach: the prover will attempt to prove the autoformalized theorems, successful proofs will be collected, and the prover will be fine-tuned on these proofs to enhance its capabilities.
c28e95a06dfcf13fc65a1cac83722f53e34f12a5.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on mathematical competition datasets, specifically the MATH dataset (12,500 problems) and the miniF2F benchmark (488 problems with human formalizations in Isabelle). BLEU scores will be used to quantitatively compare the quality of autoformalizations against human references, and manual evaluation will be performed to classify translation success and failure modes. The neural theorem prover (Thor) will be fine-tuned using proofs generated from the autoformalized statements, and its performance will be evaluated on the miniF2F benchmark using proof success rates as the primary metric. Baseline comparisons will include previous state-of-the-art neural theorem provers and prior benchmarks such as PACT and FMSCL. The experimental setup will utilize greedy decoding for LLM outputs, and all experiments will be run on high-performance computing resources (e.g., TPUv3).
c28e95a06dfcf13fc65a1cac83722f53e34f12a5.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces a novel application of large language models for the autoformalization of natural language mathematics into formal theorem prover code, demonstrating that LLMs can successfully formalize a significant portion of competition-level mathematical problems. The methodology further innovates by using these autoformalized statements to generate new training data for neural theorem provers, enabling a self-improvement cycle via expert iteration. This results in a new state-of-the-art performance on the miniF2F theorem proving benchmark, surpassing previous methods. The work also provides a detailed analysis of the strengths and limitations of LLM-based autoformalization and explores the prospects of back-translation for further improvements.

c2c438832f28e3bf5f3200808eb20e2fc7a1fd70.title: Revealing and Mitigating Over-Attention in Knowledge Editing
c2c438832f28e3bf5f3200808eb20e2fc7a1fd70.research_question: How can the problem of specificity failure in knowledge editing for large language models be mitigated, especially when edited entities appear in the context, without compromising the accuracy and generalization of the edited knowledge?
c2c438832f28e3bf5f3200808eb20e2fc7a1fd70.hypothesis: Specificity failure in knowledge editing is primarily caused by excessive attention (attention drift) to edited entities, and introducing a targeted regularization mechanism that restricts such attention drift during the editing process will significantly reduce specificity failure while maintaining high edit success and generalization.
c2c438832f28e3bf5f3200808eb20e2fc7a1fd70.proposed_method: A novel method, Selective Attention Drift Restriction (SADR), will be developed to address specificity failure in knowledge editing. The approach involves first identifying attention heads that exhibit excessive attention drift by comparing attention weight distributions before and after editing. During the knowledge editing optimization, a regularization term will be dynamically applied to only those attention heads that show over-attention to the edited subject, constraining their attention weights to remain close to their pre-editing distributions. The SADR objective will be integrated into existing knowledge editing frameworks, such as locate-then-edit methods, by augmenting the loss function with a KL-divergence-based penalty on the selected attention heads. The method will be designed to be lightweight, flexible, and compatible with a variety of editing paradigms and model architectures.
c2c438832f28e3bf5f3200808eb20e2fc7a1fd70.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on a suite of large language models, including GPT-J-6b, Llama3-8b, and GPT-NeoX-20b, covering a range of model sizes and architectures. The evaluation will utilize a combined dataset of 1,683 factual statements from COUNTERFACT and WikiData, with additional tests on QA-format and recent knowledge editing benchmarks. Baseline comparisons will include prominent knowledge editing methods such as ROME, MEMIT, and PMET, representing locate-then-edit, parameter-preserving, and meta-learning paradigms. Metrics will assess rewrite efficacy, generalization, specificity (including RelationScore and DistractNeighborhoodScore), and fluency, with specificity measured both in standard and context-injected scenarios. The experimental setup will include ablation studies on head selection strategies and hyperparameter trade-offs, and statistical significance will be reported using confidence intervals.
c2c438832f28e3bf5f3200808eb20e2fc7a1fd70.novelty_claims: The proposed method introduces a targeted, dynamic regularization mechanism that selectively constrains only those attention heads responsible for excessive attention drift, rather than applying uniform restrictions. This approach is the first to systematically diagnose and mitigate specificity failure in knowledge editing by directly addressing the causal role of attention drift. The method is lightweight, model-agnostic, and can be flexibly integrated into existing editing frameworks. Experimental results are expected to demonstrate substantial improvements in specificity metrics—often exceeding 50% relative gains—while incurring minimal loss in edit success and generalization, establishing a new state-of-the-art in safe and precise knowledge editing.

c2c7da6e0dde4b3e91de1d3e574d875f6c10a864.title: Euler Characteristic Transform Based Topological Loss for Reconstructing 3D Images from Single 2D Slices
c2c7da6e0dde4b3e91de1d3e574d875f6c10a864.research_question: How can the incorporation of topological priors improve the reconstruction of 3D images from single 2D slices, particularly in domains with limited data availability?
c2c7da6e0dde4b3e91de1d3e574d875f6c10a864.hypothesis: Integrating a topological loss function based on the Euler Characteristic Transform (ECT) into the training of neural networks will enhance the quality and topological correctness of 3D reconstructions from single 2D slices, outperforming purely geometric loss functions and existing topology-based regularizers.
c2c7da6e0dde4b3e91de1d3e574d875f6c10a864.proposed_method: A novel topological loss function will be developed based on the Euler Characteristic Transform (ECT), which captures global topological features such as connectivity, tunnels, and voids in 3D shapes. The ECT-based loss will be computed by first converting predicted and ground-truth 3D images into cubical complexes, then evaluating their Euler Characteristic Curves along multiple sampled directions and thresholds. The loss will be defined as the average L2 distance between the ECTs of the predicted and ground-truth images across these directions and thresholds. This topological loss will be combined with a standard geometric loss (such as DICE loss) and used as the objective for training a neural network (e.g., SHAPR) for 3D reconstruction from single 2D slices. The method is designed to be computationally efficient, injective, and compatible with any neural network architecture.
c2c7da6e0dde4b3e91de1d3e574d875f6c10a864.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on two publicly available biomedical datasets: Red Blood Cells (RBC) and Nuclei, both consisting of 3D images with limited sample sizes. The proposed method will be evaluated by incorporating the ECT-based loss into the SHAPR neural network and compared against two baselines: the original SHAPR model (using only geometric loss) and SHAPR with a Wasserstein-based topological loss. Evaluation will use 5-fold cross-validation with a 60%/20%/20% train/validation/test split, and metrics will include Intersection-over-Union (IoU) error, relative volume error, and relative surface error. Data augmentation (random flips and rotations) will be applied during training, and Otsu's thresholding will be used for binarization during testing. Hyperparameters such as the number of ECT directions, thresholds, and loss scaling will be tuned for optimal performance.
c2c7da6e0dde4b3e91de1d3e574d875f6c10a864.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces a new, computationally efficient topological loss function based on the Euler Characteristic Transform that is provably injective and stable under certain conditions. Unlike prior topological losses based on persistence diagrams, the ECT-based loss retains more location information and is better suited for binary images. The method can be seamlessly integrated into any neural network architecture and is demonstrated to significantly improve 3D reconstruction quality, especially in data-limited biomedical settings. Theoretical analysis is provided for the injectivity and stability of the loss, and empirical results show substantial improvements over existing geometric and topological loss functions.

c2cc96eed844bac516c95039cb3a175761fc5d2d.title: Improved Finite-Particle Convergence Rates for Stein Variational Gradient Descent
c2cc96eed844bac516c95039cb3a175761fc5d2d.research_question: What are the finite-particle convergence rates of the Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) algorithm in both the Kernelized Stein Discrepancy (KSD) and Wasserstein-2 metrics, and how do these rates depend on the number of particles, dimension, kernel, and potential assumptions?
c2cc96eed844bac516c95039cb3a175761fc5d2d.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that by analyzing the evolution of the joint density of particle locations and its relative entropy with respect to the product target measure, improved and near-optimal finite-particle convergence rates for SVGD can be achieved in both KSD and Wasserstein-2 metrics, potentially matching i.i.d. rates under mild regularity assumptions.
c2cc96eed844bac516c95039cb3a175761fc5d2d.proposed_method: The proposed method involves tracking the time evolution of the relative entropy between the joint density of N SVGD particle locations and the N-fold product of the target distribution, starting from a regular initial distribution. By decomposing the time derivative of this relative entropy into a dominant negative term proportional to N times the expected KSD squared and a smaller positive term, explicit convergence rates for the expected KSD are derived. For continuous-time SVGD, this approach yields O(1/sqrt(N)) convergence in KSD, and the method is extended to discrete-time SVGD by carefully controlling discretization errors and introducing a parameter to interpolate between exponential and Gaussian tail behaviors. Additionally, by augmenting the kernel with a bilinear component and leveraging recent theoretical connections, the method is further extended to obtain finite-particle convergence rates in the Wasserstein-2 metric, particularly for kernels of the 'bilinear + Matérn' type.
c2cc96eed844bac516c95039cb3a175761fc5d2d.experiment_details: The experimental plan includes theoretical analysis and derivation of convergence rates for both continuous-time and discrete-time SVGD under various kernel and potential assumptions. Theoretical results will be validated by comparing the derived rates to known i.i.d. rates and to previous bounds in the literature, such as those by Shi and Mackey (2024). The analysis will consider polynomial and dimension-dependent rates, and the dependence on initialization and kernel choice will be explicitly characterized. Empirical experiments may be conducted on synthetic datasets with known target distributions (e.g., Gaussian, mixtures) to numerically verify the predicted convergence rates in KSD and Wasserstein-2 metrics. Baselines for comparison will include previous SVGD convergence results and i.i.d. sampling rates, with evaluation metrics being the empirical KSD and Wasserstein-2 distances between the empirical and target distributions.
c2cc96eed844bac516c95039cb3a175761fc5d2d.novelty_claims: The proposal introduces a novel analytical framework for finite-particle SVGD that achieves near-optimal O(1/sqrt(N)) convergence rates in KSD, representing a double exponential improvement over previous results. The approach does not require strong tail assumptions on the target distribution and provides explicit dimension dependence. For the first time, finite-particle convergence rates in the Wasserstein-2 metric are established for non-Gaussian SVGD dynamics using bilinear + Matérn kernels, revealing a curse-of-dimensionality analogous to the i.i.d. setting. The method also establishes marginal convergence and long-time propagation of chaos for time-averaged particle laws, providing a comprehensive theoretical understanding of finite-particle SVGD behavior.

c2d29e2b10572d229e83e8c0005f9b48223332eb.title: Mitigating Neural Network Overconfidence with Logit Normalization
c2d29e2b10572d229e83e8c0005f9b48223332eb.research_question: How can the overconfidence of neural networks, particularly in distinguishing in-distribution from out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, be effectively mitigated to improve OOD detection and confidence calibration without sacrificing in-distribution classification accuracy?
c2d29e2b10572d229e83e8c0005f9b48223332eb.hypothesis: Enforcing a constant norm on the logit vectors during training will decouple the influence of logit magnitude from network optimization, leading to less overconfident predictions and improved separability between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.
c2d29e2b10572d229e83e8c0005f9b48223332eb.proposed_method: A novel training objective, Logit Normalization (LogitNorm), is proposed as a replacement for the standard cross-entropy loss. This method normalizes the logit vector (the pre-softmax output of the neural network) to have a constant Euclidean norm during training, effectively removing the influence of logit magnitude on the optimization process. The softmax cross-entropy loss is then computed on these normalized logits, with an input-dependent temperature parameter controlling the magnitude. The approach is implemented by dividing the logits by their L2 norm (plus a small epsilon for numerical stability) before applying the softmax and cross-entropy loss. This normalization encourages the network to focus on the direction of the logits rather than their magnitude, resulting in more conservative and distinguishable confidence scores for in-distribution and OOD inputs.
c2d29e2b10572d229e83e8c0005f9b48223332eb.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using standard image classification benchmarks, specifically CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as in-distribution datasets, and six common OOD datasets: Textures, SVHN, Places365, LSUN-Crop, LSUN-Resize, and iSUN. Neural network architectures such as WRN-40-2, ResNet-34, and DenseNet-BC will be employed. The performance of LogitNorm will be compared against models trained with standard cross-entropy loss, as well as alternative regularization and normalization approaches (e.g., Logit Penalty, GODIN, Cosine Loss). Evaluation metrics will include FPR95 (false positive rate at 95% true positive rate), AUROC, AUPR for OOD detection, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for confidence calibration. Both the maximum softmax probability (MSP) and advanced OOD scoring functions (ODIN, Energy, GradNorm) will be used for comprehensive assessment. Hyperparameters such as the normalization temperature will be tuned using a validation set, and results will be averaged over multiple random seeds.
c2d29e2b10572d229e83e8c0005f9b48223332eb.novelty_claims: The proposed LogitNorm loss introduces a simple yet effective modification to the training objective that enforces a constant logit norm, directly addressing the root cause of neural network overconfidence. This approach is broadly applicable to different architectures and compatible with various post-hoc OOD scoring functions, significantly improving OOD detection performance and confidence calibration without degrading in-distribution accuracy. Unlike prior normalization or penalty-based methods, LogitNorm achieves superior separability between in-distribution and OOD samples and is straightforward to implement within existing deep learning frameworks.

c2df739133b8d6617c4a2ff46decbea5092b27a9.title: Private Stochastic Convex Optimization with Heavy Tails: Near-Optimality from Simple Reductions
c2df739133b8d6617c4a2ff46decbea5092b27a9.research_question: How can differentially private stochastic convex optimization be performed efficiently and accurately in the presence of heavy-tailed gradients, under minimal moment assumptions on the Lipschitz constants of sample functions?
c2df739133b8d6617c4a2ff46decbea5092b27a9.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that by leveraging reduction-based techniques and novel localization frameworks, it is possible to design differentially private algorithms for stochastic convex optimization that achieve near-optimal excess loss rates (up to logarithmic factors) even when only kth-moment bounds on the Lipschitz constants are available, rather than uniform bounds.
c2df739133b8d6617c4a2ff46decbea5092b27a9.proposed_method: The proposed methodology develops a suite of reduction-based algorithms for differentially private stochastic convex optimization (DP-SCO) under heavy-tailed gradient assumptions. The approach introduces a population-level localization framework combined with geometric aggregation, enabling the use of constant-probability guarantees to boost weak subproblem solvers to high-probability solutions. The core algorithm employs a clipped differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) subroutine, where gradient clipping is used to control sensitivity and ensure privacy, while a careful analysis bounds the bias introduced by clipping using only kth-moment information. For settings where Lipschitz constants are known, a reduction to the uniform Lipschitz case is performed by thresholding and replacing outlier samples, enabling the use of existing optimal DP-SCO algorithms. For smooth functions and generalized linear models, the method further incorporates stability analysis and the sparse vector technique to ensure privacy of gradient step counts, resulting in efficient (near-linear or linear time) algorithms.
c2df739133b8d6617c4a2ff46decbea5092b27a9.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets exhibiting heavy-tailed distributions, with varying moment bounds and dimensionalities. The proposed algorithms will be compared against state-of-the-art baselines for DP-SCO under both uniform and heavy-tailed Lipschitz assumptions, including clipped stochastic gradient methods and recent population/localization-based approaches. Evaluation metrics will include the excess population loss, privacy guarantees (in terms of (ε, δ)-differential privacy and concentrated DP), and computational efficiency (runtime, gradient queries). Key experimental setups will vary the moment parameter k, privacy parameters (ε, δ), and problem smoothness to assess robustness and optimality of the proposed methods.
c2df739133b8d6617c4a2ff46decbea5092b27a9.novelty_claims: The proposed research introduces the first algorithms for heavy-tailed DP-SCO that achieve near-optimal excess loss rates up to logarithmic factors, under minimal kth-moment assumptions on Lipschitz constants. The localization framework and geometric aggregation strategy are novel in their ability to boost constant-probability subproblem solvers to high-probability solutions without requiring strong uniformity or smoothness assumptions. The method also provides the first optimal and efficient algorithms for known-Lipschitz and smooth heavy-tailed settings, including linear-time solutions for generalized linear models. The integration of the sparse vector technique within optimization algorithms to ensure privacy of internal operations is an additional innovation with potential independent interest.

c2f91f35df893714418cc29096083dce0b441229.title: Neural Codec Language Models are Zero-Shot Text to Speech Synthesizers
c2f91f35df893714418cc29096083dce0b441229.research_question: Can a language modeling approach, utilizing discrete codes from a neural audio codec, enable high-quality, zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis for unseen speakers using only a short acoustic prompt?
c2f91f35df893714418cc29096083dce0b441229.hypothesis: A neural codec language model, trained as a conditional language model on large-scale, diverse speech data and using discrete audio codec codes as intermediate representations, will enable zero-shot TTS synthesis that matches or exceeds state-of-the-art systems in terms of naturalness and speaker similarity, even for unseen speakers with minimal enrollment data.
c2f91f35df893714418cc29096083dce0b441229.proposed_method: A novel TTS framework will be developed that treats speech synthesis as a conditional language modeling task over discrete audio codec codes rather than continuous signal regression. The method will employ a pre-trained neural audio codec (such as EnCodec) to quantize speech into discrete codes, which serve as the intermediate representation. The system will consist of a hierarchical language model: an autoregressive (AR) transformer for the first quantizer's codes, conditioned on both phoneme sequences and a short acoustic prompt, and a non-autoregressive (NAR) transformer for subsequent quantizers, conditioned on previous codebooks, phoneme prompts, and acoustic prompts. During inference, a 3-second enrolled recording from an unseen speaker will be encoded as the acoustic prompt, and the model will generate the corresponding discrete codes for the target text, which are then decoded back to waveform using the neural codec decoder. The approach enables in-context learning and prompt-based zero-shot TTS synthesis without additional fine-tuning or complex speaker encoders.
c2f91f35df893714418cc29096083dce0b441229.experiment_details: The proposed system will be pre-trained on the LibriLight dataset, comprising 60,000 hours of English speech from over 7,000 speakers, using automatically generated phoneme transcriptions. Evaluation will be conducted on LibriSpeech (test-clean) and VCTK datasets, ensuring all test speakers are unseen during training. Baselines will include the state-of-the-art zero-shot TTS system YourTTS, as well as speech-to-speech models like GSLM and AudioLM. Evaluation metrics will include word error rate (WER) for content fidelity, speaker similarity scores using a top-performing speaker verification model (WavLM-TDNN), and human evaluations for naturalness (CMOS) and speaker similarity (SMOS). Ablation studies will assess the impact of different prompt types and model components. The experimental setup will use large-scale distributed training on GPUs, and both automatic and crowdsourced human evaluations will be performed.
c2f91f35df893714418cc29096083dce0b441229.novelty_claims: The proposed method is the first to treat TTS as a language modeling task over discrete neural audio codec codes, enabling strong in-context learning and prompt-based zero-shot synthesis akin to GPT-3 for text. It leverages an unprecedented scale of semi-supervised speech data for TTS, demonstrating that large-scale data alone can yield robust generalization to unseen speakers. The framework eliminates the need for fine-tuning, pre-designed acoustic features, or complex speaker encoders, and is capable of preserving speaker identity, emotion, and acoustic environment from short prompts. The approach enables diverse output generation and achieves state-of-the-art performance in both naturalness and speaker similarity for zero-shot TTS.

c2fbc8ad4e2403c795529c2606e4686f5a571215.title: From attribution maps to human-understandable explanations through Concept Relevance Propagation
c2fbc8ad4e2403c795529c2606e4686f5a571215.research_question: How can explanations for deep neural network predictions be made more human-understandable by unifying local and global perspectives, thereby addressing both where and what questions in model inference?
c2fbc8ad4e2403c795529c2606e4686f5a571215.hypothesis: Combining local attribution methods with global concept-based explanations will yield explanations that are more interpretable and actionable for human users, enabling deeper insights into model reasoning and facilitating the identification of spurious correlations and biases.
c2fbc8ad4e2403c795529c2606e4686f5a571215.proposed_method: A new framework, Concept Relevance Propagation (CRP), will be developed to extend traditional Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) by enabling conditional backpropagation of relevance scores associated with human-understandable concepts encoded in hidden layers. CRP will disentangle the relevance flows for specific concepts, allowing the computation of concept-conditional relevance maps that localize both the spatial origin and semantic meaning of features used in individual predictions. Additionally, a Relevance Maximization (RelMax) approach will be introduced to select representative input samples where latent features are maximally relevant (rather than merely maximally activated) for a given prediction, thus providing faithful, outcome-specific examples for each concept. The method will support post-hoc analysis of arbitrary neural network architectures without requiring changes to model training or data labeling, and will allow for the construction of concept atlases, composition graphs, and quantitative analyses of concept subspaces.
c2fbc8ad4e2403c795529c2606e4686f5a571215.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on multiple datasets, including ImageNet and other domains such as time series data, using standard deep neural network architectures like VGG-16 (with and without BatchNorm). The proposed CRP and RelMax methods will be compared against established local XAI techniques such as LRP, Integrated Gradients, SHAP, and Grad-CAM. Evaluation will include qualitative analyses (e.g., visualization of concept atlases, composition graphs, and detection of Clever Hans artifacts), quantitative studies (e.g., measuring the contribution of concept subspaces to predictions), and a human user study assessing interpretability and utility of explanations. Metrics will include human accuracy in identifying model reliance on artifacts, clarity and confidence ratings, and computational efficiency. Baselines will consist of traditional attribution maps and activation maximization approaches.
c2fbc8ad4e2403c795529c2606e4686f5a571215.novelty_claims: The proposed approach uniquely unifies local and global XAI perspectives by enabling concept-conditional relevance propagation, thereby answering both where and what questions for individual predictions. CRP and RelMax provide post-hoc, model-agnostic explanations that do not require specialized architectures, labels, or training regimes. The methods enable the construction of concept atlases, facilitate the identification and mitigation of spurious correlations (Clever Hans effects), and allow for fine-grained analysis of concept subspaces and their roles in decision making. Human studies demonstrate superior interpretability and practical utility over existing XAI methods, and the framework is computationally efficient and broadly applicable.

c3066a2fac7cb7e9ee4d5b8d4eba9d3e2d20bd87.title: Statistical Query Lower Bounds for List-Decodable Linear Regression
c3066a2fac7cb7e9ee4d5b8d4eba9d3e2d20bd87.research_question: What are the fundamental computational limits of list-decodable linear regression when the majority of data points are adversarially corrupted, and what is the complexity of this problem in the Statistical Query (SQ) model?
c3066a2fac7cb7e9ee4d5b8d4eba9d3e2d20bd87.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that list-decodable linear regression with a majority of adversarial outliers is computationally hard in the SQ model, requiring either exponentially many queries, exponentially large output lists, or queries with extremely fine tolerance, thereby matching or nearly matching the best known algorithmic upper bounds.
c3066a2fac7cb7e9ee4d5b8d4eba9d3e2d20bd87.proposed_method: The proposed research will develop a rigorous lower bound for the problem of list-decodable linear regression in the SQ model. This will be achieved by constructing a family of distributions over labeled examples (X, y), where X is drawn from a high-dimensional Gaussian and y is a noisy linear function of X, with a fraction α of inliers and the rest adversarial outliers. The methodology will leverage the SQ dimension framework for search problems over distributions, focusing on constructing large sub-families of distributions that are nearly uncorrelated with respect to a carefully chosen reference distribution. The construction will involve moment-matching techniques, using linear programming duality to ensure that the mixture of inlier and outlier distributions matches many low-degree moments of the reference distribution, while maintaining bounded χ2-divergence. Additional technical innovations will address the challenge of matching moments when the outlier fraction approaches one for large values of y, by adjusting the reference distribution to have heavier tails and carefully balancing the outlier fraction across different regions.
c3066a2fac7cb7e9ee4d5b8d4eba9d3e2d20bd87.experiment_details: The research will theoretically analyze the SQ complexity of list-decodable linear regression, providing lower bounds on the number of queries, the tolerance required, and the size of the output list. Theoretical results will be compared against known algorithmic upper bounds, such as those achieved by the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) hierarchy and other recent algorithms, which require d^{poly(1/α)} samples and time. The evaluation will focus on the regime where the inlier fraction α is less than 1/2, and the regression vector has bounded norm, with additive Gaussian noise. Key metrics include the minimum number of SQ queries, the minimum tolerance achievable, and the minimum list size required to guarantee that at least one hypothesis is close to the true regression vector. No empirical datasets are used; all results are proven theoretically.
c3066a2fac7cb7e9ee4d5b8d4eba9d3e2d20bd87.novelty_claims: The proposed research establishes the first strong SQ lower bounds for list-decodable linear regression with a majority of adversarial outliers, showing that any SQ algorithm must use either exponentially many queries, exponentially large lists, or extremely fine tolerance. The construction introduces a novel moment-matching approach via linear programming duality, enabling the matching of poly(1/α) many moments even in the challenging regime where the outlier fraction is close to one. The results provide evidence that current algorithmic upper bounds are nearly optimal within the SQ model, and the techniques developed may have broader implications for other robust learning problems and related computational models, such as low-degree polynomial algorithms.

c346bfb9b2e2730ee3aa392fd17956416191e38d.title: Diversify Your Vision Datasets with Automatic Diffusion-Based Augmentation
c346bfb9b2e2730ee3aa392fd17956416191e38d.research_question: How can dataset diversity for fine-grained visual classification tasks be automatically increased to improve generalization across unseen domains, such as changes in context, weather, or location, without requiring expensive manual data collection or user-supplied prompts?
c346bfb9b2e2730ee3aa392fd17956416191e38d.hypothesis: Automatically generating and applying natural language-guided image augmentations, grounded in the original training data and filtered for data integrity, will yield more effective and diverse training datasets than traditional augmentation or text-to-image generation, leading to improved model generalization and robustness.
c346bfb9b2e2730ee3aa392fd17956416191e38d.proposed_method: A novel data augmentation framework will be developed that leverages large pretrained vision and language models to automatically generate domain-specific natural language descriptions from a given labeled dataset. The process begins by captioning each image using a pretrained image captioning model, then summarizing these captions into a concise set of domain descriptions using a large language model (LLM). These domain descriptions are used to guide text-conditioned image editing of the original training images via diffusion-based models, such as Stable Diffusion (Img2Img) or InstructPix2Pix, to create new, contextually diverse but visually consistent augmentations. To ensure the quality and relevance of the augmented data, a two-stage filtering process is applied: first, a CLIP-based semantic filter removes images unrelated to the task; second, a confidence-based filter using a classifier trained on the original dataset removes images that are either minimally changed or have corrupted class-relevant information. The resulting augmented dataset is then used to train downstream classifiers.
c346bfb9b2e2730ee3aa392fd17956416191e38d.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on three benchmark datasets: CUB (fine-grained bird classification), iWildCam (domain generalization in animal classification), and Waterbirds (contextual bias mitigation). The proposed method will be compared against several baselines, including models trained on the original data, traditional augmentations (CutMix, RandAugment), text-to-image generated data, and real data from the test distribution. For each method, the number of augmented images per class will be matched, and hyperparameters will be tuned for optimal validation performance. Evaluation metrics will include classification accuracy and class-balanced accuracy, with results averaged over multiple random seeds. Additional ablation studies will assess the impact of prompt quality, filtering strategies, editing methods, and the amount of augmented data added.
c346bfb9b2e2730ee3aa392fd17956416191e38d.novelty_claims: The proposed framework introduces a fully automated, language-guided image augmentation pipeline that does not require user-supplied prompts or fine-tuning of generative models. By grounding both the domain descriptions and image edits in the original training data, the method produces visually consistent and contextually diverse augmentations tailored to the task. The approach combines vision-language models for domain summarization, diffusion-based image editing, and a novel two-stage filtering process to ensure data integrity. This results in augmented datasets that outperform traditional augmentation and text-to-image generation, and in some cases, even surpass the addition of real data from unseen domains.

c35c41dc9c93eff38ec8913cb4d639b06a915d33.title: Linear attention is (maybe) all you need (to understand transformer optimization)
c35c41dc9c93eff38ec8913cb4d639b06a915d33.research_question: What are the fundamental optimization characteristics of Transformer models, and can a simplified linearized Transformer abstraction serve as a realistic and effective testbed for understanding the unique challenges in Transformer optimization?
c35c41dc9c93eff38ec8913cb4d639b06a915d33.hypothesis: A shallow, linearized Transformer model—without nonlinear activations or feedforward networks—can reproduce the distinctive optimization features observed in full Transformer models, thereby providing a valuable abstraction for studying and understanding Transformer optimization dynamics.
c35c41dc9c93eff38ec8913cb4d639b06a915d33.proposed_method: A linearized, shallow Transformer architecture will be developed, omitting nonlinear activations and feedforward layers, and parameterized using single query-key matrices for simplicity. The model will be trained on random instances of linear regression tasks, where covariates and target weights are sampled from specified distributions (e.g., Gaussian, heavy-tailed). The linear self-attention mechanism is defined without the softmax operation, and multiple layers can be stacked to explore depth effects. The optimization objective is to predict a missing target value in the regression context, using the output of the final linear attention layer. The model's training dynamics will be analyzed under various data distributions and architectural depths to investigate the emergence of Transformer-specific optimization phenomena.
c35c41dc9c93eff38ec8913cb4d639b06a915d33.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted using synthetic datasets generated from random linear regression problems, with covariates sampled from both standard Gaussian and heavy-tailed (Gamma-scaled) distributions. Several experimental settings will be explored, varying the number of context examples, covariate dimensionality, and the number of Transformer layers (e.g., L=2,4,6,8). Baseline comparisons will include adaptive optimizers (Adam) and non-adaptive methods (SGD, with and without momentum), with hyperparameters selected via grid search. Evaluation metrics will focus on training loss curves, the distribution of stochastic gradient noise, robust condition numbers of the loss landscape, and directional smoothness along optimization trajectories. Multiple random seeds will be used for statistical robustness, and additional experiments will test the effects of nonlinear data transformations and parameterization variants.
c35c41dc9c93eff38ec8913cb4d639b06a915d33.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces a minimal yet realistic linearized Transformer abstraction that captures all major optimization phenomena previously observed in full Transformer models, including the superiority of adaptive methods (Adam > SGD), heavy-tailed gradient noise, ill-conditioned loss landscapes, and unique smoothness properties. This abstraction enables controlled, interpretable experiments that are infeasible with full-scale Transformers, providing new insights into the roles of data distribution and model depth in shaping optimization dynamics. The work establishes a concrete, tractable testbed for future theoretical and empirical studies on Transformer optimization, potentially guiding the development of more effective training methods.

c37f5eb5998f4110d07501fde9f94363c13a441f.title: 3DGS-Drag: Dragging Gaussians for Intuitive Point-Based 3D Editing
c37f5eb5998f4110d07501fde9f94363c13a441f.research_question: How can intuitive, efficient, and high-quality point-based drag editing be achieved for geometry-related content manipulation in real 3D scenes?
c37f5eb5998f4110d07501fde9f94363c13a441f.hypothesis: Integrating explicit 3D Gaussian splatting-based deformation guidance with diffusion-based appearance correction, combined with a progressive multi-step editing strategy, enables precise, consistent, and visually realistic point-based 3D drag editing across diverse scenes.
c37f5eb5998f4110d07501fde9f94363c13a441f.proposed_method: A novel framework is developed that leverages a pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model to represent the scene, enabling explicit manipulation of 3D geometry. The method takes as input a set of user-specified 3D handle points and corresponding target points, and applies a deformation strategy to the Gaussians near each handle point, using translation and interpolated rotation to approximate the desired geometric change. Deformation is performed in a copy-and-paste manner, preserving original Gaussians with reduced opacity for flexibility. After deformation, rendered images from multiple views are corrected using a fine-tuned 2D diffusion model (Dreambooth with LoRA), which is iteratively updated to ensure multi-view consistency and remove artifacts. A progressive, multi-step editing scheduler divides the drag operation into intervals, relocating handle points and updating the diffusion model at each step to support aggressive and large-scale edits.
c37f5eb5998f4110d07501fde9f94363c13a441f.experiment_details: Experiments are conducted on eight scenes drawn from established datasets including Instruct-NeRF2NeRF, PDS, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temple. The editing process uses 50 selected views per scene, focusing on those with maximal visibility of the edited region. Baselines for comparison include Instruct-NeRF2NeRF, PDS, SDE-Drag, and a deformation-only approach. Evaluation metrics include qualitative visual inspection, user preference studies with 19 participants, and GPT-4o-based scoring for both editing effectiveness and rendering quality. Ablation studies are performed to assess the impact of local editing masks and the number of progressive drag steps. The method is benchmarked for efficiency, with editing times reported on a single RTX 4090 GPU.
c37f5eb5998f4110d07501fde9f94363c13a441f.novelty_claims: The proposed approach introduces the first point-based 3D drag editing framework for real scenes that bridges deformation-based geometric guidance and diffusion-based appearance correction. Key innovations include a copy-and-paste deformation strategy for 3D Gaussians, a multi-view consistent diffusion-guided correction mechanism, and a progressive multi-step editing scheduler with handle point relocation and history-aware diffusion fine-tuning. The method enables a wide range of geometry-related edits (motion, shape, inpainting, extension) with high efficiency and visual quality, outperforming prior 3D editing techniques in both capability and speed.

c39fb7a46335c23f7529dd6f9f980462fd38653a.title: Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model
c39fb7a46335c23f7529dd6f9f980462fd38653a.research_question: Can an agent achieve high performance in complex planning and visually rich domains, such as Atari games, Go, chess, and shogi, without access to the underlying environment dynamics or game rules by leveraging a learned model for planning?
c39fb7a46335c23f7529dd6f9f980462fd38653a.hypothesis: It is hypothesized that an agent can achieve superhuman or state-of-the-art performance in both planning-intensive and visually complex domains by learning a model that predicts only the quantities directly relevant to planning (reward, policy, and value), rather than modeling the full environment dynamics or observations.
c39fb7a46335c23f7529dd6f9f980462fd38653a.proposed_method: A novel reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed that integrates model-based planning with a learned model, enabling effective decision-making without access to the true environment dynamics. The method consists of three core neural network components: a representation function that encodes past observations into a hidden state, a dynamics function that updates the hidden state and predicts immediate rewards given hypothetical actions, and a prediction function that outputs the policy and value from the hidden state. Planning is performed using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) over the learned model, where at each node, the model predicts the policy, value, and reward for hypothetical future actions. The entire model is trained end-to-end by minimizing the error between the predicted and target policy, value, and reward, using targets generated by MCTS and observed rewards from real environment interactions. The approach does not require the hidden state to reconstruct the original observation or match the true environment state, focusing instead on optimizing for accurate planning.
c39fb7a46335c23f7529dd6f9f980462fd38653a.experiment_details: Experiments will be conducted on a diverse set of domains, including all 57 games in the Atari Learning Environment and the board games Go, chess, and shogi. The proposed method will be trained for 1 million mini-batches, with batch sizes of 2048 for board games and 1024 for Atari, using 800 MCTS simulations per move for board games and 50 for Atari. The neural network architecture will employ convolutional and residual blocks, with 16 residual blocks and 256 hidden planes. Baseline comparisons will include state-of-the-art model-free algorithms such as R2D2, IMPALA, Rainbow, LASER, and previous model-based approaches like SimPLe. Evaluation metrics will include mean and median human-normalized scores for Atari, and Elo ratings for board games, with performance assessed against both human and algorithmic baselines.
